en: The Bhāṭṭatantrarahasya, composed by the venerable Ācārya Khaṇḍadeva, who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the glorious Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā; the opening invocation of auspiciousness.
By repeatedly remembering the enemy of Mura and by relying upon His grace,
we are able to clarify the secret of the Bhaṭṭa-tantra.
Khaṇḍadeva is now prepared to reveal that secret by which the statement of Jaimini regarding the promise of what is to be accomplished becomes clearly manifest in its true essence.

In that regard, within the *Twelve-Lakṣaṇī*, Jaimini has investigated only dharma and adharma for their utility in ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). Although dharma and adharma consist of specific types of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and are not themselves of the nature of action (*kriyā*), nevertheless—in passages such as "Dharma perishes through [failure to] proclaim it," and because the terms "dharma" and "adharma" are used in the Vaiśeṣika system to denote the unseen merit produced by action—nevertheless, in passages such as "Dharma, when performed by men...
and because the terms "dharma" and "adharma" are also applied to the enjoined and prohibited actions that produce them, these two are investigated here primarily as such.
The Rejection of the Definition of Dharma and Adharma:

Now, what indeed is meant by "dharma-ness" or "adharma-ness"? It is certainly not the state of being an enjoined action, nor is it the state of being a prohibited action; for that [definition] would fail to apply to enjoined or prohibited substances and the like. Indeed, [the definition would exclude] those who perform auxiliary rites for the sake of a result, as well as those who employ silver and other such items in a sacrifice.

If it were so, there would be no distinction in worldly discourse between "righteous" (*dhārmika*) and "unrighteous" (*adhārmika*). Furthermore, in that case, there would be no connection with the scriptures in sections such as the *Indriyakāmādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning one who desires sensory power). Moreover, if that [action] lacked the nature of *dharma*, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by it would lack the nature of *dharma*, and consequently, it could not be destroyed by public proclamation (*kīrtana*). Nor is it the case that it lacks the nature of action (*kriyātva*); for if it did, then speaking untruth for the sake of marriage—which is the subject of a rule of permission—would result in being *dharma*, and the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup would result in being *adharma*.
[Response: This is an explanation of the definitions of *dharma* and *adharma* by way of refuting the aforementioned objections.

No; for the definition of Dharma is simply "that which has the status of being a means to the highest good (śreyaḥ) as taught by the Veda," and the definition of Adharma is "that which has the status of being a means to the undesirable (aniṣṭa) as taught by that [Veda]. This is because such definitions are logically consistent. For the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the eating of *kalañja* (a type of poison), and so forth, have their status as means to the desirable and the undesirable taught by the Veda; thus, the definition applies there. Here, the phrase "taught by the Veda" is included to exclude Brahman, heaven, hell, and the like, as these also possess the quality of being taught by the Veda. Furthermore, the first part of the definition is included to exclude the eating of poison and similar acts, even though they possess the status of being means to the desirable and the undesirable, because they are not taught by the Veda.
Regarding the objection and resolution concerning the *dharmaness* of the Śyena sacrifice:

since it is precisely the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) that is taught by the Veda in the case of the Śyena, it is indeed *dharma*. However, the quality of producing an undesirable result belongs only to the *abhicāra* (malevolent rite) consisting of acts such as striking with a weapon, which is conducive to the death of an enemy—the very fruit of the Śyena. And because that [rite] alone possesses the quality of being a means to an undesirable end as taught by the Veda, it is *adharma*, but not the Śyena itself; this is clearly explained in the fourth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra].

This constitutes the refutation of the doubt that the sacrifice, which is a means to the death of an enemy, is *adharma*, as well as the description of the defining conditions (*upādhi*) for *dharmaness* and *adharmaness*.

However, where there is an injunction such as, "One desiring the death of an enemy should sacrifice," even there, because the injunction makes known that [the act] is a means to a desired end, the sacrifice and so forth are indeed *dharma*. Nor is it the case that the sacrifice itself falls under the scope of the prohibition "one shall not harm," on the grounds that it is an activity conducive to death; for since the prohibition is satisfied by referring to harm prompted by worldly desire (*rāga*), it does not apply to what is enjoined. Furthermore, it does not follow that, in such cases, the learned would engage in the act without hesitation—just as they do with the *śyena* sacrifice—due to the non-arising of demerit (*pratyavāya*) even through a mediated sequence.

By reflecting on such statements as, "That which is for the purpose of destroying another is declared to be tāmasa," it follows that even the *abhicāra* rite—which generates malevolent magic (*abhicāra*)—is censured as being *tāmasa*. Consequently, by the force of the prohibition inferred therefrom, such an act is indeed *adharma* because it produces undesirable results, even though it is prescribed for the sake of a specific fruit; thus, there is no contingency of its being [unaccountably] so. For this very reason, since *dharma*-ness and *adharma*-ness are merely conditional attributes (*upādhi*), there is no fault even if they overlap. This concludes the presentation and refutation of the point stated in the *Arthasaṃgraha* and other texts.

As for the claim that because the definition of dharma includes being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānubandhitva*), and since this is absent in the *śyena* sacrifice and similar acts, they are not dharma—that is incorrect. This is because there is no purpose in including such a factor; furthermore, "powerfulness" consists in the intensity of aversion toward the undesirable, which depends on past karma, and thus the absence of such a connection could occur even in the *śyena* at some times. Otherwise, due to the lack of causal completeness (*sāmagrī*) in the *śyena*, its performance would never be possible.

Furthermore, if the Śyena sacrifice and others lacked the nature of *adharma*, it would be untenable to describe them as having the nature of *tāmasa-dharma* (darkness-based dharma). Therefore, the aforementioned two definitions apply correctly even in those cases. Moreover, by means of a permissive injunction (*abhyanujñā-vidhi*), there is merely the implication of the absence of fault; since this does not imply that [the act] is a means to a desired end, even though lying is prompted by desire, it does not result in being *dharma* because it lacks the status of being a means to a desired end as cognized by the Veda.

Furthermore, in the case of the prohibition regarding the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, there is no implication that it is a means to an undesirable result (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*), because there is a lack of evidence and because such an assumption would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Rather, even in its absence, the mere accomplishment of the great benefit for the sacrifice through the other constituent parts [is sufficient]; since the person's desistance is logically established by that much alone, it follows that for the sake of inducing activity therein, the injunction implies an abundance of fruit. Therefore, even in that case, there is no occurrence of unrighteousness (*adharmatva*).

And "being cognizable by the Veda" means being cognizable by the Veda while not being independently cognizable by any means of knowledge other than the Veda; therefore, even though the knowledge of Brahman—which consists of the direct realization of reality—is cognizable by the Upaniṣads, it does not follow that it is *dharma*, since its status as the generator of liberation—consisting in the cessation of ignorance along with its manifestations regarding Brahman—is established by other means of knowledge.

Even if it is held that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is not an effect of ignorance because it is real, and that liberation—consisting of the destruction of the twenty-one types of suffering and so forth—is produced by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), such a view is nonetheless authoritative; nevertheless, since the fact that [liberation] is generated by [the knowledge of reality] cannot be known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one must set aside "being taught by the Veda" and instead provide "being taught by an injunction" (*vidhi*) in order to exclude its being a *dharma*. For knowledge, being dependent on the object as it is established by a means of valid cognition, is not an object for instigation (*pravartanā*), and thus it cannot be what is taught by an injunction.

In reality, however, since the word *dharma* is used even for knowledge in such passages as, "This indeed is the supreme *dharma*: the perception of the Self through yoga," there is no harm in its being a *dharma*. Nor is the word "perception" (*darśana*) in that context intended to mean meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), because there is no evidence for such a figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, it is impossible for meditative absorption—which consists of the cessation of mental fluctuations—to be produced by yoga in the primary sense. And just like ritual worship (*upāsanā*) and the like, although knowledge is a *dharma*, the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsā*) is distinct from the inquiry into *dharma* (*dharmamīmāṃsā*), because Brahman lacks the status of being a *dharma*—that is, it does not possess the quality of being a means to the highest good as defined by the Veda.

Or, let it be that "being pervaded by human effort" is added as a qualification to the definition of dharma in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman; since even a quality (*guṇa*), when qualified by its substratum, is pervaded by effort, there is no lack of extension (*avyāpti*). Furthermore, this applies to knowledge (*jñāna*) as well in its own nature.

Even though [the Self] lacks being pervaded by an action (*kṛti*), there is no lack of definition (*avyāpti*), because—just as in the case of proper digestion and so forth—it is possible for that which is entered by the action to be pervaded by the action through a mediated sequence, since the mental application (*manaḥpraṇidhāna*) conducive to that [Self-realization] is itself pervaded by the action. For this very reason, it can also be easily stated in this system that the injunctive suffix in the passage "The Self, indeed, is to be seen" has this same intention. Alternatively, one should include "uncommon causality" (*asādhāraṇī kāraṇatā*) within the definition.

The respective definitions themselves are the delimiters of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for the words *dharma* and *adharma*; and since these two words, *dharma* and *adharma*, apply by means of a single power (*śakti*) common to both action and the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by it, they refer respectively to action and the unseen merit/demerit produced by it—this is the summary.
Thus ends the investigation into the definition of dharma in the *Bhāṭṭatantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Khaṇḍadeva.
Now, regarding the theory of injunction (*vidhivāda*):
establishing the nature of being a means (*sādhanatva*) as a constituent of the definition of *dharma*.

Objection: Since there is no word expressive of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), how can the fact that sacrifice is a means to the highest good (*śreyassādhanatva*) be understood through the Veda in such passages as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*)? And what, moreover, is an injunction (*vidhi*)? If it is asked: "What is that which makes the fact of being a means to the highest good something to be understood [by the Veda]?"
Regarding the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), this is the view of the logicians (*tārkika*):

Here, the logicians maintain that since an inclination to act is observed immediately after hearing the optative suffix and so forth, there is no dispute that the cognition of the optative suffix and so forth is useful for the inclination to act by way of generating the causal complex for that inclination. And that causal complex consists of a desire characterized by the mode "to be accomplished by an effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva-prakārikā icchā*), which is the desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*). Since that [desire-to-act] functions as a cause in its actual existence, even if the cognition of the optative suffix and so forth is not directly useful for it, its utility is postulated for the cognition that serves as the cause of the desire-to-act.

And that [cause of activity] consists of the cognition that [the action] is not followed by an undesirable result of greater weight, the cognition that it is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), and the cognition that it is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). For even if the other two are present, if any one of these three is absent—as in the case of eating food mixed with honey and poison, touching the moon, or performing the *maṇḍalī* gesture—no inclination toward activity is observed. Therefore, since the cognition of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth generates this triad of cognitions, the expressive power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix and the like resides in its being not followed by an undesirable result of greater weight, its being achievable through effort, and its being a means to a desired end. Furthermore, regarding those [three], the qualifier...

In the absence of a specific qualifier (*viśeṣya*), due to the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), there is a denotative power (*śakti*) for each [element]. Just as in the case of the word *puṣpavanta*, because of the diversity of linguistic derivation (*vyutpattivaicitrya*), there is a simultaneous cognition of all three meanings.
In the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), this constitutes the inclusion of the objects associated with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*liṅ*).

And its syntactic connection (anvaya) occurs, by virtue of semantic fitness (yogyatā), with the meaning of the verbal root itself—such as sacrifice—in cases like [the injunction] "one should sacrifice"; and in cases such as "one should not eat *kalañja*," it connects with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), namely non-existence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, that [non-existence] does not pertain to all three [properties] of the act of eating *kalañja*, because eating *kalañja* is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhya*) and is a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhana*). Rather, it pertains specifically to the property of not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). Therefore, in that case, the absence of the property of not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence—that is, the property of being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence—is understood through the negation; and due to the absence of the cause [for action], there is no inclination toward it. Consequently, that [act] possesses the nature of demerit (*adharma*), whereas sacrifice and the like possess the nature of merit (*dharma*).

They say that in the case of the Śyena sacrifice and others, there is a syntactic connection (anvaya) only with "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhya*) and "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), but not with "not being followed by a powerful undesired consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). This is because, through another means of knowledge, the result of that sacrifice—which is the act of sorcery (*abhicāra*)—is understood to be a cause of hell; thus, it possesses the nature of being followed by a powerful undesired consequence in the form of its being a producer of hell. Consequently, those who are believers (*āstika*) do not engage in it. This concludes the refutation of the Naiyāyika position.

That is not so; for it is cumbersome to postulate three potencies (*śakti*), and because it is an empirical fact that activity occurs through the mere cognition of a thing being a means to a desired end, even in the absence of the cognition that it is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). Therefore, the cognition that an action is followed by a powerful undesirable consequence is an obstacle to activity, and its absence is a cause only insofar as it exists in its own right (*svarūpasat*). Consequently, since the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others are of no use there—just as desire itself is not—the optative suffix does not have that [absence] as its denotation.

Furthermore, in this way, the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by the word *nañ* is the cause for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the "lack of connection with a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), which is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as co-occurring with *nañ*. The mental presentation generated by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the cause for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the optative suffix as co-occurring with *nañ*, provided that it is distinct from the "lack of connection with a powerful undesirable consequence. The mental presentation generated by the verbal root is the cause for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the optative suffix as co-occurring with *nañ*.

There are seven causal relations [of cognition]: (1) the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case is the cause for a verbal cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is the meaning of *nañ* co-occurring with an optative suffix (*liṅ*); (2) the presentation generated by a verbal root (*dhātu*) is the cause for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of *nañ* co-occurring with an optative suffix; (3) the presentation generated by a word ending in the nominative case is the cause for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the effort (*kṛti*) denoted by a verb ending (*ākhyāta*) not co-occurring with *nañ*; (4) the presentation generated by the word *nañ* is the cause for a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the effort denoted by a verb ending co-occurring with *nañ*. These are the seven causal relations.

Furthermore, if this were the case, then upon the presence of the negative particle (*nañ*) in co-occurrence with the optative suffix (*liṅ*), the meaning of the suffix—namely, the state of not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*)—would be construed there [with the negative]. However, for the meaning of the suffix other than that [i.e., the positive form], it would always be construed with the root-meaning; and when the negative particle is absent, it would likewise be construed with the root-meaning. Thus, one would fall into the error of postulating a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) based on the cognition of multiple cumbersome co-occurrences.

Thus, in cases such as "the jar does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*) or "Caitra does not cook" (*na pacati caitraḥ*), when there is no co-occurrence with an optative suffix (*liṅ*) or the like, the negation (*nañ*)—whose meaning is absence—is construed with the substratum presented by the nominative case-ending word. However, when there is co-occurrence with an optative suffix or the like, it is construed with the verbal root-meaning itself; thus, there is a multiplicity of grammatical rules (*vyutpatti*). Similarly, in the absence of *nañ*, the meaning of the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*), such as effort (*kṛti*), is construed with the substratum presented by the nominative case-ending word through the relation of substratum-hood (*āśrayatā-sambandha*); but when *nañ* is present, it is construed with that [verbal] meaning.

"By means of the relation of being the counter-positive," [they argue], "the causal relations (kāryakāraṇabhāva) become cumbersome. This is for the sake of the meaning of the statement, "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice. This is the demonstration of parsimony (*lāghava*) according to the Mīmāṃsaka school.

In our view, however, there is parsimony: according to the method to be explained, when the negative particle (*nañ*) is absent, the two meanings of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) are connected to the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) by the relation of being prompted (*prayojyatva*); when it is present, they are connected by the relation of being the counter-positive of an absence prompted by itself (*svaprayojyābhāvapratiyogitva*). Furthermore, the meaning of *nañ* is everywhere connected to the meaning of the verbal suffix—namely, the effort (*kṛti*)—by the relation of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*), and the meaning of the nominative term is connected to that effort by the relation of subsistence (*ādheyatva*). Thus, there are four relations, or according to the method to be explained, only one; hence there is parsimony.

Furthermore, in the case of the injunction "one should not eat *kalañja*," even if the injunction conveys that eating is not connected with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), it also conveys that it is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Since this [status as a means to a desired end] can be accounted for by taking ordinary worldly satisfaction, its [further] specification would result in redundancy; thus, on your view, there would be the contingency of postulating heaven according to the *Viśvajit* principle. However, since one may postulate hell—which is superior to that [heaven]—there is no contradiction with its being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence.

For this very reason, where there is no way at all to avoid the futility [of an injunction] regarding the cognition that something is to be accomplished by effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), it is not even inconsistent for it to be a mere restatement of what is already established in common worldly usage.

Furthermore, if all three [properties] constitute the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), then why is there no cognition of the "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice? If you say it is because of sublation (*bādha*), then what is this so-called "sublation"? If you say that the very fact that the *abhicāra* (sorcery), which is the fruit of the *śyena*, falls within the scope of the prohibition "one shall not kill" due to its nature as violence (*hiṃsā*) constitutes the sublation, we reply: since that [prohibition] is a general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*), it fulfills its purpose even by taking recourse to violence prompted by passion (*rāga-prāpta-hiṃsā*), just as in the case of killing an animal for a sacrifice. Therefore, the property of "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" in the *śyena* must be understood specifically...

Since [the Śyena sacrifice] is measured by a scriptural injunction, one does not engage in it even for the sake of accomplishing that [desired result]; furthermore, even if one were somehow to engage in it, there would be no contradiction between the two [desires], because one would not postulate an additional hell resulting from the malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).

Moreover, let us examine the nature of "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). It cannot mean "not producing a pain greater than the pain that is an unavoidable concomitant of the arising of the desired object," because even when the knowledge of that [status] exists due to a scriptural injunction, we do not observe engagement in sacrifices and the like by the indolent person or the one who hates the expenditure of their own wealth; thus, such knowledge is not a cause for engagement.

Even though one knows—on the basis of prohibitive scripture—that the consumption of *kalañja* and similar acts produces an excess of suffering that is inseparable from the desired result, a person driven by passion still engages in such acts; therefore, that knowledge does not function as an obstacle to activity.

Therefore, "the state of being a powerful undesirable" (*balavadaniṣṭatva*) means being the object of intense aversion (*utkaṭadveṣa*). This intensity is a specific type [of aversion] that is to be inferred solely from its effects; and such aversion occurs in accordance with past karma. Consequently, even regarding the suffering produced by sacrifices and the like, when there is intense aversion due to the force of past karma, then—because of the presence of the cognition that it is connected to a powerful undesirable—the person does not engage in it. However, when there is no intense aversion due to the force of auspicious karma, then—because of the absence of the cognition that it is connected to a powerful undesirable—the activity toward it occurs due to the absence of an obstructing factor.

Thus, in cases such as the eating of *kalañja* (a forbidden vegetable) and the *śyena* sacrifice, occasional engagement or non-engagement must be explained solely by the force of past karma. Consequently, since it is impossible for an injunction (*vidhi*) to invariably convey the property of "not being connected with a powerful undesirable result" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) regarding sacrifices and the like, and since it is impossible for a negative particle (*nañ*) to invariably convey the absence of that property regarding the eating of *kalañja* and the like, the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth do not have their primary denotative power (*śakti*) in those instances.
If one does not accept that the suffix has the meaning of an injunction, then [the functions of] bringing about an undesirable consequence and its removal [would be untenable].

As for the argument that—since the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) does not consist in being "not connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*)—the worldly sentence "One desiring satisfaction should eat *kalañja*" would incur the status of being authoritative (because the meaning of the injunction, in the form of "being a means to a desired end" and so forth, other than "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence," is not sublated therein); whereas in our view, its lack of authority is established because it is taught by scripture (*śruti*) that [eating *kalañja*] is indeed connected with a powerful undesirable consequence—[this objection is as follows].

That is not so; for while that consequence would follow according to the view of those who maintain that the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) consists in being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) qualified by not being followed by a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), it does not follow according to the view that the meaning of an injunction is *pravartanā* (incitement). To explain: in the absence of the negative particle (*nañ*), it will be stated that the aforementioned *pravartanā* connects with the sense of the verb (*ākhyāta*), namely "effort" (*kṛti*), through the relation of being prompted (*prayojyatva*). Furthermore, that "being prompted" is defined as being prompted by an inference generated by a cognition whose object is itself (*svaviṣayakajñānajanyānumitiprayojyatva*). This [inference] occurs when the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) in an action such as sacrifice is not known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In that case, there is an inference of the knowledge of instigation (*pravartanā*) precisely from the fact of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). However, where that [fact of being a means to a desired end] is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and its status as a means to an undesired end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*) is also established by a prohibition—as, for example, in the case of eating the food of one consecrated for a sacrifice (*dīkṣita*), due to the prohibition "One should not eat the food of one consecrated"—there, the subsequent injunction "When the omentum has been offered, one may eat the food of the consecrated" implies only the absence of its being a means to an undesired end, and not its being a means to a desired end; for that...

Because no inference arises when there is an absence of the desire to prove [the conclusion] due to its being established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even the knowledge that something is not a means to an undesired end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*) is useful for activity, insofar as it causes one to ascertain the invalidity of a knowledge that takes as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) that very thing which is the object of that [knowledge].

For in the case of activity, it is precisely the cognition that [an act] is a means to an undesired end—which is not overridden by a cognition of its invalidity—that acts as the obstacle when there is a state of intense aversion. Consequently, when that [cognition] results in the ascertainment of invalidity, its utility toward activity is easily established by way of producing the absence of that qualified [cognition]. And thus, since an injunction whose object is the subject matter of a prohibition—being of the nature of a mandatory injunction—implies only the absence of being a means to an undesired end regarding its own object, and since that [absence] is sublated in the case of a worldly statement by contradiction with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), the establishment of its invalidity is logical; therefore, that much [is not required].

The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is the state of not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). Nor is "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*) the meaning of the optative; for in your view, since the suitability of cooking for effort is understood in the same cognition as the effort itself, it follows that "being achievable through effort" is also understood regarding the cooking. Thus, because it is obtainable from another source, it cannot be the denotation of the optative suffix and so forth. In our view as well, since the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is established through the implication of the incitement (*pravartanā*), just like the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and so on, it too is obtainable from another source. Therefore, by process of elimination, it must be stated that the meaning of the optative suffix and so forth is precisely the status of being a means to a desired end.

The refutation of the view that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is "being a means to what is desired" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) follows: some moderns indeed accept this very position. However, in cases involving the co-occurrence with the negative particle (*nañ*), there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "being a means to what is undesired" (*aniṣṭasādhanatā*) by the optative; therefore, the meaning of the optative and so forth is exclusively "being a means to what is desired. That too is not correct, because activity proceeds from the mere cognition of being a means to what is desired. Otherwise, in instances such as "I am bringing the cow because I am urged by my teacher," the conventional designation of the teacher and others as the "instigator" (*pravartaka*) would be untenable. Nor is it the case that [the instigator is] the utterer of the optative which conveys the state of being a means to what is desired, which generates the activity.

Therefore, the conventional designation of that [king] as the "instigator" (*pravartaka*) is based on his being the cause of the instigation. If it were otherwise, then a foot-soldier urged by the king would himself become an instigator by virtue of being the utterer of such a *liṅ* (injunctive suffix), and consequently, the conventional usage—expressed as "I am not acting out of being urged by the foot-soldier, but rather out of being urged by the king"—which indicates the absence of the status of an instigator in the foot-soldier, would be untenable.

Now, if one defines an instigator as "one who utters such a *liṅ* while not being urged by another," then even so, the king would fail to be considered an instigator when he is urged by a sycophant (*piśuna*).

Therefore, by the force of such linguistic usage, the status of being an instigator (pravartakatva) on the part of a king or similar authority must be stated as consisting precisely in being the locus of the desire that is the object of the cognition which serves as the cause of activity. Nor is it possible for there to be such a cognition even if desire were not denotable by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; for although a particular object may be a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), since it lacks the status of being the object of another's desire, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and thus its being a means to a desired end could not logically serve as an inferential mark (*anumāpaka*). Consequently, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), that [desire] alone must be denotable by the optative suffix and so forth; and thus, with respect to the object of activity...

In the case of sacrifice and the like, since the understanding [of its status] is established by inference alone—namely, that it is a means to a desired end—there is no occasion for postulating that it is directly denoted [by the optative suffix]. For being the object of the desire of a trustworthy person (āpta) in the form "let this person proceed toward this" is pervaded by being a means to a desired end; therefore, the latter is inferred from the former. This is the statement of the purpose of the constituent parts of the logical reason.

In this context, although there exists the state of being an object of a desire such as "May happiness arise for me" regarding what is actually not happiness—due to the delusion that it is happiness, or regarding actual happiness itself—the term *ākāraka* (the qualifier) is pursued up to its limit within the definition of the reason (*hetu*) in order to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in those cases, since they lack the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Furthermore, the term *āpta* (reliable/authoritative) is included to exclude deviation in the case of such an object of desire that serves merely as a mode (*prakāratā*).

In this context, "being the object of desire" should be understood as being the object of an inclination that has become the object of a desire. Consequently, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) even if the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is absent in the case of the inclination itself, or in the person who is its substratum, provided they are objects of desire. Furthermore, it is precisely in the case of sacrifices and the like that the inference of being a means to a desired end occurs because the probans is present there.
Regarding the investigation into the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*):

although, according to the method to be explained, either "activity-ness" (*vyāpāratva*) or "desire-ness" (*icchātva*) is the delimitor of the denotative capacity of the optative suffix and so on, nevertheless, by that...

The cognition of desire in the manner described above arises from words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), because the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with specific verbal roots and suffixes acts as the regulator. For instance, in the sentence "I shall make a vessel out of clay," there occurs a cognition having a particular earthen vessel as its qualificand in its general form as a "vessel," due to the co-occurrence [of the word *pātram*]. Furthermore, due to the capacity for action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*), there is a cognition of the person who is the locus of the activity; and once the speaker's reliability is understood through their speech, gestures, and so forth, the fact that the desire resides in that reliable person is also cognized.

Because it is cognizable by the same cognition (*samānasaṃvitsaṃvedyatā*), there is an understanding of its being the object of such a desire (*tādṛśecchāviṣayatva*) in the case of sacrifices and the like; thus, there is no lack of proof for the reason (*hetvasiddhi*). Consequently, once the knowledge of the cause has arisen through the aforementioned collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*), the inference of "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth is easily obtained. Therefore, since "being a means to a desired end" is obtainable from other sources, it is not the meaning expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like. If "being a means to a desired end" were the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), there would be over-extension (*atiprasakti*).

Furthermore, according to your view, for one who has already engaged in cooking and the like because they understood it to be a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) through their own [cognition], there would arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of using the expression "Caitra should cook" even during the present state of that cooking. This is because the possession of an effort conducive to cooking qualified by being a means to a desired end is not sublated (*abādhitatva*) in Caitra; thus, just as in the case of "Caitra cooks," there would be no harm even if the presentness were not conveyed. In my view, however, since such an engagement is not prompted by an injunction (*preraṇā*), the lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*) of such an expression is established due to the sublation of its object (*viṣayabādha*). This constitutes the difference between our positions.

In the theory of instigation (*preraṇāvāda*), an objection is raised regarding over-extension (*atiprasakti*) and its refutation: "Indeed, even in your own view, where Caitra's activity is prompted by another's instigation, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the sentence 'Caitra should cook' being valid during the state when the cooking is already present; for the activity residing in Caitra conducive to the cooking remains unimpeded in its being produced by that instigation."

In reality, even an activity produced by the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end—which is established intrinsically—is susceptible to being prompted by an instigation (*preraṇā*) due to its inherent fitness to be so prompted; therefore, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one could say "Caitra should cook" would be unavoidable. For, according to you, an effort (*kṛti*) qualified by being prompted [by an instigation] as realized through a result does not appear in verbal cognition, since in many cases activity does not arise from verbal cognition due to laziness and other factors. If this is argued, we reply: No.

Injunction (*preraṇā*) is not the causal factor for activity (*pravṛtti*) as such, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); rather, it is the causal factor for activity as qualified by occurring subsequent to an injunction. This is because of universal worldly usage such as: "This activity is prompted by an injunction; this one is not, but is [prompted] spontaneously."

In this very context, another alternative may be described: it can also be said that *preraṇā* (instigation) is simply another property (*dharmāntara*) that is subsumed under the nature of activity (*pravṛttitva*) by virtue of being the delimitor of its being prompted (*prayojyatāvacchedaka*). For this very reason, it will also be stated that *preraṇātva* (the essence of instigation), as the delimitor of its being the prompter (*prayojakatāvacchedaka*), is an indivisible property (*akhaṇḍadharma*) common to both worldly and Vedic usage.

Furthermore, in cases where there is co-utterance with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, that property which is pervaded by "being an activity" is understood from the verb ending (*ākhyāta*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), or else the instigation (*preraṇā*) is presented as the individual to be prompted under the very form of a general property; such are other [details]. In any case, regarding an activity produced by the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end established by itself, the instigation does not function as a prompter even by way of its own nature; thus, there is no contingency of employing a sentence containing an optative suffix toward one who already possesses such an activity. This explains the avoidance of using the expression "one should cook" (*pacet*) at a time when an activity prompted by instigation is already occurring.

However, the undesirable consequence that would arise when an activity prompted by an instigation is currently occurring can be avoided in this way: we do not assert that the instigation is construed with the activity solely through the relation of being its object (*viṣayatā-sambandha*).

Nor is it the case that [the instigation] is the object of the activity in the sacrifice and so forth, such that one might fear the occurrence of such a linguistic usage. Rather, for this very reason, by abandoning the direct relation, the instigation functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the activity denoted by the verbal suffix, through the relation of being "prompted by an inference produced by its own cognition. For there exists a causative efficacy (*prayojakatva*) on the part of the inference of being a means to the desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), which is produced by the cognition of the instigation, with respect to the activity, because it acts as its generator. This will be demonstrated further below.

The knowledge of instigation (*preraṇājñāna*) is introduced into the middle of the relation as being, by its very nature, something to be produced by a cognition of itself occurring at a time prior to itself, and as being that particular instance [of such a cognition]. The first occurrence of the word "self" (*sva*) refers to each specific instance of the activity, while the second occurrence of "self" refers to each specific instance of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. Consequently, the resultant meaning is this: the relation consists in the fitness (in the sense of being capable of producing) the state of being prompted by an inference of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatvānumiti*), which is produced by that knowledge of the word "optative" etc. which occurred at the time of the prior absence of each respective activity. And therefore—

In our view, since there is no sublation of the property of being prompted by this relation during the state of the activity's actual occurrence, such an undesirable linguistic application does not arise.

As for the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in reference to others at a time prior to an activity prompted by the instigation of another—such as when foot-soldiers or other trustworthy persons are seen using the optative during a time of activity prompted by a king—this is not to be raised as an objection, as it is a desired outcome (*iṣṭāpatti*). For in such cases, the usage can indeed occur by taking the king’s instigation as the basis, as well as by taking the instigation of others; this is because even an inference generated by knowledge of that [instigation] is capable of inducing activity. Therefore, it is established that, contrary to the method of the logicians (*tārkika*), the meaning of the optative and similar suffixes is not "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth, but rather, according to the aforementioned reasoning, it is simply the desire that prompts action.
Demonstration of Pāṇini’s agreement with the theory of instigation (preraṇāvāda), and an exposition of the other meanings of the injunctive suffix (vidhi).

Regarding the rule *Pāṇini* 3.3.161, "The *liṅ* and *loṭ* [moods] are used in the senses of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), entreaty (*āmantraṇa*), request (*adhīṣṭa*), inquiry (*sampraśna*), and prayer (*prārthana*); and in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the *leṭ* is used in the sense of the *liṅ*," this very meaning is understood. *Vidhi* (injunction) is the instigation of one who is inferior. *Nimantraṇa* (invitation) is a desire on the part of an instigator that leads to the inference that non-performance would result in an undesirable consequence. For example, the instigation of a daughter's son (*dauhitraka*) and others at a *śrāddha* ceremony and similar rites, because through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), one understands that there is sin (*pratyavāya*) in not eating [there].

For this very reason, as in the case of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), the two subsequent [factors] also merely infer that [the action] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) due to parsimony; the inference of being achievable by effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) applies everywhere. Or, let that [inference] be absent. An invitation (*āmantraṇa*) is permission for acting according to one's own will; in that case, there is merely the absence of insistence on the part of the instigator.

Demonstrating Pāṇini’s agreement with the theory of instigation (*preraṇāvāda*), and explaining the other meanings of the injunctive suffixes: from Pāṇini’s grammatical rules such as "The *liṅ* and *loṭ* [suffixes] are used in the senses of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), permission (*āmantraṇa*), request (*adhīṣṭa*), inquiry (*sampraśna*), and entreaty (*prārthana*); and in the Veda, 'the *leṭ* is used in the sense of the *liṅ*'," this very meaning is understood. Injunction (*vidhi*) is the instigation of one who is inferior [to the speaker].

*Nimantraṇa* (an invitation) is the desire of an instigator that leads to the inference of the status of being the counter-positive of a non-performance which would result in an undesirable consequence. For example, the instigation of a daughter’s son (*dauhitr*) and others at a *śrāddha* ceremony and similar rites; for in those cases, it is understood through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in not eating [the offered food]. Therefore, just as in the case of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), in the two subsequent cases as well, there is simply the inferential indication of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) due to parsimony (*lāghava*). The inferential indication of being achievable by an effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) applies to all [three] alike—or let that be disregarded. *Āmantraṇa* (a request) is permission for acting according to one's own will.

In that case, there is merely the state of insistence on the part of the instigator; elsewhere, however, even greater insistence appears. *Adhīṣṭa* (authorization) is the instigation of a superior preceded by honor. Since the single factor of "instigating" (*pravartanatva*) is common to these four, there is only one power (*śakti*) in that very form; as for the other components, they are not part of the denotable meaning (*śakyatva*) because they are obtainable through other means of knowledge. However, in the cases of *saṃpraśna* (inquiry) and *prārthanā* (request), the power is indeed distinct.

However, in cases such as "But you should study," "My request is that you study the Veda," and so forth, the nature of instigation (*pravartanātva*) is absent. Alternatively, it is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), just as in the case of causality and the like according to grammatical rules such as "The *liṅ* suffix occurs in the sense of cause and effect" and "The *kaccit* suffix occurs in the expression of a wish. This is because, through extensive usage, the nature of instigation itself is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, the nature of instigation is the state of being an operation conducive to activity; and conduciveness is the state of being a generator. And that [generativity] resides, in the world, in the mental disposition (*āśaya*) of a person, while in the Veda...
Therefore, it should be understood that something distinct from desire possesses the nature of an instigation (*pravartanātva*).

Regarding this point, Maṇḍana Miśra holds the view that even in the Veda, it is precisely the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) that constitutes the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, in its form as an instigation. Pārthasārathi, however, maintains that the power (*śakti*) residing in the optative suffix itself—which is conducive to the denotation of the objective productive activity (*arthabhāvanā*)—is designated by the term "denotation" (*abhidhā*); having postulated that this very power is expressed by the optative suffix in the form of an instigation, he posits that the mere cognition of it is the cause for the initiation of action.

In reality, however, there is an absence of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) between being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*); for if that were the case, then even in common worldly usage, that [latter] alone would result in being such [a motivator], leading to the consequence of the aforementioned refutation of the Naiyāyika view. Furthermore, even in the theory of the "power to impel" (*śaktipravartanāvāda*), whether one considers the power of the optative suffix (*liṅtva*) or the power conducive to the expression of number (*saṃkhyābhidhānānukūlaśakti*), the absence of a decisive reason remains exactly as it was.

Therefore, by the maxim that "when there is no decisive evidence [for choosing between alternatives], another [factor] is postulated [only] when those already established are insufficient," it is the extraordinary *dharma* (merit) residing in the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth that is postulated as the inciting force (*pravartanā*), and it is that which is denoted by the optative suffix and the like; furthermore, the knowledge of that [dharma] is the cause for activity. Thus, the view of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* alone is somehow tenable, as clarified in the *Kaustubha*. This concludes the determination of the operation (*vyāpāra*) as being denoted by the optative suffix.

In reality, however, desire does not function as a cause for activity in its own essential form (*svarūpeṇa*), because activity arises even in its absence through a misconception of it; furthermore, if it were a cause in its own essential form, the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) would be redundant. Nor does the cognition of that [desire] serve as the cause, since it functions merely as an inferential indicator (*anumāpaka*) of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

Since the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is established by the fact that [the word] is merely the motivator (*prayojaka*) with respect to a specific activity (*pravṛtti*), there is no evidence for postulating its status as a cause (*kāraṇatva*). Therefore, "incitement-ness" (*pravartanātva*) must be defined simply as being the motivator of activity. Furthermore, even this cannot be the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, because it is cumbersome (*gaurava*) and because it is obtainable through other means (*anyalabhya*).

For *pravṛtti* (activity) is indeed obtained from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) itself; however, the status of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*) is obtained through the force of syntactic relation (*saṃsarga*), and thus it does not enter into the category of the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Rather, it is simply the nature of being an operation (*vyāpāratva*) that serves as the delimitor of denotability, common to both worldly and Vedic usage. For in the worldly case, there exists in the human intention (*puruṣāśaya*)—which is presented by words such as the optative (*liṅ*) and which serves as the means for activity—the state of being an operation that instigates activity, by way of inferring [the agent's] belief that the action is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

Even in the case of the Veda, since one observes its effect only after hearing the word and inferring it through reasoning—and because desire is impossible in the non-human (apauruṣeya) Veda—one postulates an extraordinary property (*dharma*) residing in the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, which is inferable from the effect and denoted by the optative suffixes. Because that [property] is assumed to be the indicator of the [action], it also possesses the status of being an operation (*vyāpāra*) that motivates activity. Therefore, the common factor for both [human and Vedic injunctions] is simply "the state of being an operation" (*vyāpāratva*), which serves as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

And although that [over-extension] would apply elsewhere as well, nevertheless, a specific [meaning] is obtained through the force of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*). To explain: even though from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) there arises the apprehension of a mere operation (*vyāpāra*) delimited by the property of being an operation, once it is understood that this [operation] is related to the "effort" (*kṛti*) denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) via the aforementioned relation, then at the time of the cognition of that relation in its specific form, the acquisition of the particular [operation] through the respective means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not difficult to obtain. For this is indeed accepted.

In cases such as "the ground is like a pot," although the word "pot" brings about the cognition of the pot alone as delimited by the universal *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness), when that [pot] is construed with the ground through a possible relation, and there arises a desire to know that relation in its specific nature, there occurs— just as one cognizes a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as being of the nature of conjunction and so forth by means of another pramāṇa— the cognition of a specific pot residing on the ground.
This is the presentation of the manner in which that specific [object] is obtained.

Thus, the sequence here is as follows: first, there is the presentation of the operation (*vyāpāra*) in its general form as suchness from the word *liṅ* (the optative suffix) and so forth. Subsequently, that [operation] is construed with the *kṛti* (volitional effort) presented by the finite verb (*ākhyāta*), through the relation of being prompted by an inference generated by a specific cognition whose object is itself, even though it is not presented as suchness. And the verbal comprehension is: "The volitional effort regarding sacrifice and so forth possesses the operation."

Furthermore, one should not fall into the error of thinking that verbal cognition (śābdabodha) has only the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as its qualificandum. This is because, in accordance with the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating "the verb (*ākhyāta*) has the action (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning," and out of deference to the parsimony (*lāghava*) of postulating a single cause-and-effect relationship—where the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by the verbal form is the cause for a verbal cognition delimited by having the meaning of the *lakāra* suffix as its qualifier, related to it by the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*)—the *kṛti* (volitional effort), which is the meaning of the verb, alone possesses the status of the primary qualificandum.
The following is the demonstration of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the remaining meanings of the optative suffix.

In the case of inquiry (*sampraśna*) and request (*prārthanā*), that [suffix] is also construed with that very [action] through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā-sambandha*). Even though causality (*hetutva*) and so forth are also construed with it through the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), that [causality] is construed with another action by way of being a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇatva*) and so on. Alternatively, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) has the function of indicating the intention regarding the relation consisting in the state of having a cause (*hetumattva*). Therefore, in cases such as *ārtim ārchet* ("he might suffer harm"), the construction of the meaning of the verbal suffix itself with another action occurs precisely through the relation of having a cause; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. This also establishes the possibility of the construction of the expression of desire (*kāmapravedana*).

Similarly, in cases such as "If one should eat rice, then one should pour curds [over it]," even though the *liṅ* suffix expresses a desire (*kāmapravedana*), the relation is that of being caused by a desire directed toward its own object; here, the *liṅ* serves to indicate the speaker's intention. Alternatively, the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) itself may indicate the desire, while in the case of "If one should wish to eat rice," the relation is simply that of being a cause. Thus, there is no need for a separate theory of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) in any instance.

And therefore, in cases such as "Devadatta should cook" in common worldly usage, after the verbal comprehension has occurred, when there arises a desire to know the nature of one's own connection [to that action], the fact that the activity (*vyāpāra*) consists of a volition (*icchā*) is understood through the force of such conventional expressions as "I am cooking, prompted by Caitra. Furthermore, because of the connection between the cooking and the effort (*kṛti*), it is established that the volition takes the form "May this cooking proceed. When the person who prompts the action—the elder (*prayojaka-vṛddha*)—is known to be trustworthy (*āpta*) through other means of knowledge, then, by virtue of being cognized within the same act of consciousness, [it is understood that] regarding this cooking...

A mental cognition arises whose object is the knowledge of the cause—consisting in being the object of an effort that is the content of the desire of a trustworthy person expressed in the form "Let it proceed. Then, based on that cause, through the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between being a means to a desired end and being achievable by effort (established by the example of other actions), an inference arises having both as its objects.
This concludes the investigation into the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the injunctions for obligatory rites (*nityakarman*).

In some cases, there is also the property of being the counter-positive of a non-performance that serves as a means to an undesirable end, due to the force of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). That causal complex consists of the consideration of the cause—which takes the form of the desire of the agent of the undesirable end to avoid the destruction of their own [self], expressed as "Let this person engage here"—and so forth. The word "own" (*sva*) refers to the desire; this is clear in various places such as the *Kaustubha*. Since its status as a motivator for engagement is evident, both the attainment of the relation as such and the attainment of the specific desire are easily secured.
An exposition of the nature of inference in the case of Vedic indicative marks (*liṅga*), and a definition of authoritativeness (*āptatva*) according to the Mīmāṃsaka school.

Even in the case of the Vedas, immediately after hearing words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), there arises a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of the form: "The agent's effort (*kṛti*) regarding sacrifice and so forth possesses an operation (*vyāpāra*) through the aforementioned relation," due to the presentation of the word-meaning as an operation. When there is a desire to know the nature of that relation, it is understood—both from common usage such as "Impelled by the *liṅ* suffixes in the Veda, I am performing a sacrifice," and from the relation between the effort and the object of the sacrifice—that the relation resides in the *liṅ* suffix itself and takes the form "I am instigating this sacrifice."

For this very reason, because the *liṅ* suffix consisting of phonemes is eternal, the extraordinary property (*alaukika-dharma*) residing in it is also eternal. Nor [is there any problem] by virtue of its being common to both error and valid cognition.

Since that very knowledge is the generator of the inference, there is a lack of evidence for its existence [as a distinct entity] just as in the case of worldly [knowledge]; rather, it is established through the impossibility of the knowledge arising from the Veda being an error. Furthermore, the objectivity (*viṣayitā*) regarding the sacrifice as the object of the volitional effort (*kṛti*) in that [knowledge] is neither common to the objectivity of [ordinary] knowledge and so forth, nor is it something additional; rather, it is common to the objectivity residing in worldly desires such as "May he engage in cooking," yet it is distinct from the objectivity residing in desire in general, and resides solely in the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, because of the uniform cognition [of it] therein.

Because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, once it is ascertained that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are faultless and thus distinct from those who are untrustworthy (*anāpta*), there arises a mental cognition of the reason—namely, the state of being the object of an activity residing in the agent of an instruction regarding what is beneficial or harmful that is not produced by deception, etc., and which is the object of a volition (*kṛti*) whose form is as previously described—precisely through the principle of being cognized by the same act of consciousness (*samānasaṃvitsaṃvedyatā*). For this very reason, "trustworthiness" (*āptatva*) is common to both worldly and Vedic contexts, and consists in being the author of an instruction regarding what is beneficial or harmful that is not produced by deception, etc., while not being the author of an instruction other than that [i.e., one that is deceptive].

Therefore, the inference of "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth by that [cognition] is not untenable, just as it is in the world. Nor is it the case that, in your view, the establishment of "being a means to a desired end" and so forth does not occur even in the case of sacrifice and the like, because the inference of "being a means to a desired end" etc., common to both error and valid cognition, is the motivator of activity; for in our view, since knowledge is intrinsically authoritative (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), its validity is established precisely when there is an absence of defects and the like. Furthermore, a consideration (*parāmarśa*) based on a real logical mark (*salliṅga*) does not produce erroneous inference. Thus, it is established that the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is not over-extended.
Even so, there is a specific gain regarding both worldly usage and the Veda, as well as the gain of a unique relation:
either the property of being an "unsegmented" (*akhaṇḍa*) operation is the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *liṅ*;

or rather, it is precisely this unsegmented property in the form of an operation—which is established, by the aforementioned method, as the delimitor of the causal efficiency (*prayojakatā*) for a specific inclination common to both worldly usage and the Veda—that serves as the non-overextended delimitor of the denotability of words such as *liṅ*.

The demonstration that a specific type of objectivity (*viṣayitā*) is the delimitor of the denotatum of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) by means of the example of the knowledge of speaker-intention (*tātparya*); or rather, since a specific type of objectivity common to both worldly and Vedic usage—consisting in the form "let this person be prompted here"—has been stated previously, that alone is the delimitor of the denotatum of the optative suffix and so forth. And it is precisely this method that must be accepted.

Likewise, in cases such as "Caitra should not cook" or "He should not eat *kalañja*," where the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in conjunction with the negative particle (*nañ*), it is not easily maintainable to hold the position that the meaning of the optative is "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), and that its absence is what is conveyed by the negative particle; for this view has already been refuted.

Nor is the view of the modern logicians (navīnatārkika) tenable—that there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as denoting the means to an undesirable end, and that the word *nañ* merely serves to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). For this would result in the following worldly sentence being authoritative: "One should not sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Even if the status of being a means to heaven is understood through direct audition (*śruti*), there is no contradiction in the sacrifice being a means to an undesirable end at that particular time. Indeed, there is no evidence to suggest that the meaning of a prohibition consists solely in producing an undesirable result occurring at a later time, such as hell; for this applies even to worldly sentences such as "One should not touch fire."

Because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This is because in passages such as "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," there is deviation in both ways. For if the meaning of the prohibition therein were that it is a means to an undesirable result at that time, then—even though that [prohibition] would merely be a restatement of what is established by another means of knowledge—since the statement "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*" conveys its being a means to a desirable result, the inference of the accomplishment of a great benefit for the sacrifice (*kratu*) itself would be the factor constituting the relation in that case, by means of the aforementioned inference.

Because, when the absence of engagement [in an action] is established, there is no inference therein of its being a means to an undesired result. For this very reason, in every case where a prohibition follows an injunction, what is communicated is simply the absence of the status of being a means to a desired end as cognized by the injunction; thus, even though both may possess authority through their distinct modes of application when they are Vedic, it is not untenable that a worldly statement lacks authority when it contradicts a Vedic injunction.
This concludes the refutation, following the restatement of the meaning of the preceding prohibitive statements as accepted by the Logicians (Tārkikas).

By this, it is established that when a negative particle (*nañ*) is used in conjunction with an optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, the meaning of that suffix is either by primary denotation (*śakti*) or by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) simply the non-production of suffering that is invariably concomitant with the desired result. The absence of that [non-production]—consisting in the production of such suffering—is the state of being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānubandhitva*), which is the meaning of the negative particle. And its connection is with the meaning of the verbal root. Therefore, the objection that worldly sentences would result in being invalid due to a lack of basis is refuted; for that same consequence would apply even to such Vedic injunctions as "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *Atirātra* sacrifice. This concludes the presentation of the faults in the previously mentioned positions according to the Nyāya school, and the statement of their absence in one's own system.

Furthermore, in all these positions, at the time when one who possesses passion (*rāgin*) is currently eating *kalañja*, there would be the consequence of the response being mere idle chatter regarding the connection with taste—just as in the case of the answer to the question "What is Caitra like? given as "He is one who possesses an effort conducive to eating *kalañja*, which produces pain exceeding the pain that is invariably concomitant with the attainment of the desired object," or just as in the case of the answer "One should not eat *kalañja*. Moreover, at the stage when the *śyena* sacrifice is currently occurring, there would be the consequence of the answer "One should not sacrifice with the *śyena*. However, in our own view, according to the method to be explained [later]...

There is no such undesirable consequence [of the agent's activity being inferred] because the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), which is desire, is construed with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), namely effort (*kṛti*), through the relation of being the counter-positive of an absence that occurs at a time when the causal complex for activity—produced by an inference arising from a specific cognition of that [desire]—is absent; thus, there is a difference [between this case and others].

Furthermore, this is not even an answer to the question "What is Caitra like?", because it lacks the status of having a nominative-ending term as its primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*). "What kind of... [the sentence continues].

Nor is "effort" (*kṛti*) an answer to this [question], because when the question concerns the delimiting property (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) of the locus (*liṅga*), an answer that does not involve it would be irrelevant. For this very reason, "Caitra cooks," "Caitra does not cook," and so forth, are not answers to the question "What kind of effort is it? [Otherwise,] such an answer would result in an absurdity (the *phiṃjar* fallacy). Therefore, the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*) must indeed be the effort; for otherwise, such an answer would not avoid being irrelevant.

Therefore, in instances where a negative particle (*nañ*) is employed, a "prohibition" (*nivartanā*)—just like an "impulsion" (*pravartanā*)—must be admitted as the cause of desisting, because we observe such common usage as: "I have desisted due to the teacher's instruction, not of my own accord, nor from the instruction of another. Furthermore, according to the view of the ancients, the nature of prohibition (*nivartanatva*), like that of impulsion, should be understood as a distinct property consisting in being an activity that generates desistance. And that which is delimited by this [property] is, in worldly contexts, desire (*icchā*), while in the Veda, it is a transcendental quality (*alaukiko dharmaḥ*), and so forth for all cases.

As before, the delimitor of its capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is the status of being the word *nañ*. Furthermore, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such words denoting instigation (*pravartanā*) serve as indicators of the speaker's intention (*tātparyagrāhaka*); otherwise, in cases such as "Caitra does not cook" (*na pacati caitraḥ*), there would be a cognition of absolute non-existence from the word *nañ* alone. Alternatively, it is the optative suffix that expresses the cessation of action (*nivartanā*), while the word *nañ* merely restates the absence of engagement (*pravṛttyabhāva*) and serves as an indicator of the intention; these and other points of the ancient school (*prācīnamata*) are explained clearly in the *Kaustubha*. This concludes the alternative explanation for the verbal cognition regarding the meaning of the optative suffix when it is co-occurrent with *nañ*.

In reality, however, because it would entail the postulation of multiple powers, there is no separate power for instigation (*pravartanā*) and dissuasion (*nivartanā*), nor is there a distinction between the absence of engagement and cessation; this is due to a lack of evidence and because of [theoretical] complexity (*gaurava*). Rather, the denotation of the verb suffixes (*ākhyāta*) resides solely in "action" (*kṛti*); that of the negative particle (*nañ*) resides solely in "absence"; and that of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others resides solely in the operation (*vyāpāra*) common to both instigation and dissuasion. And the delimitor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—whether it be overly broad or not overly broad—is likewise a single entity common to both instigation and dissuasion, as previously stated.

If, however, you insist that there is no single common objective domain for both instigation (*pravartanā*) and non-instigation (*nivartanā*), then let it be that the suffix *liṅ* has a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to that which is delimited by being the objective domain of cessation (*nivṛtti*), and the word *nañ* serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Furthermore, that meaning of *liṅ* is construed with the agentive sense of "effort" (*kṛti*)—which is the meaning of the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*)—precisely through the relation of being the counter-positive of an absence that is produced by an inference generated by a specific cognition whose object is itself.

The negative particle (*nañ*) also functions as an indicator of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) regarding a specific relation. Therefore, once the verbal cognition has arisen in the form, “An effort having the eating of *kalañja* as its instrument possesses the aforementioned relation,” the manifestation of that relation in its true nature occurs as before.

For here, from a knowledge concerning prohibition, there arises a knowledge of the cause—namely, that the effort is the counter-positive of an absence which is the object of the desire of a trustworthy person (the teacher) in the form, “May this person desist from the eating of *kalañja*. Through this, an inference is produced that the eating of *kalañja* is a means to an undesirable result (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*).
This is the description of the specific features in the verbal cognition arising from sentences containing injunctions and prohibitions.

Similarly, in cases such as the prohibition "one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*," when a prohibition of what has been enjoined occurs, there arises—based on the knowledge of the reason for such a subsequent injunction—an inference that the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* does not contribute to the benefit of the *atirātra*. Through this, there is also an inference that the benefit of the sacrifice is accomplished by other auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) precisely through the absence of that [cup]. And because this subsequent inference disrupts the causal complex for engagement (*pravṛtti-sāmagrī*), it serves as the cause for the non-occurrence of engagement.

To explain: where there is an inference of being a means to an undesirable end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*), if there is a powerful aversion due to the force of prior karma, this brings about the presence of an obstacle in the form of the cognition that [the act] is connected with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānubandhitvajñāna*). Consequently, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—which is constituted by the absence of that obstacle—is disrupted. This is the analysis of the connection with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).

Although in both cases the absence of the connection with an obstructer—being of the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and so forth—is eternal and thus not destructible by inference, nevertheless, because the existence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) destroys the relation of the absence, the causal-relation-delimiting relation (which consists of the *viśeṣaṇatā* relation belonging to the absence) is destroyed when the counter-positive exists; consequently, it is easily established that this [existence of the counter-positive] disrupts the causal complex for the activity [of inference]. And therefore, [the word "liṅ"] has as its meaning an inference produced by a cognition whose object is itself...

The resultant meaning is that [the action] is construed with the agentive sense (kṛti) denoted by the verbal suffix through the relation of being the counter-positive of an absence occurring at the time of the destruction of the relation that serves as the delimitor of the causality defined by the first "sva" (i.e., the meaning of the optative suffix). Here, the first occurrence of the word *sva* refers to the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), while the second occurrence of the word *sva* refers to the activity (*pravṛtti*). And in this context, there is an absolute absence of the causal complex for activity brought about by the power of fate.

To prevent the undesirable consequence that the expression "one should not eat *kalañja*" would apply at a time when there is no occurrence of [the relevant] activity, the qualification "occurring at the time of the destruction of the relation" is added. Where there is a verbal cognition of being a means to an undesired end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*) from the sentence "eating *kalañja* is a means to an undesired end," then, to prevent the aforementioned application of the expression at a stage of non-existence occurring at the time of the destruction of the relation produced by that [cognition], the qualification "produced by inference" is added to the term "destruction. [This is because the destruction is] produced by other causes of knowledge, such as the fact of following positive and negative concomitance with the undesired.

The phrase "having as its object" (*svaviṣayaka*) and so forth is included in order to prevent the undesirable consequence of such usage occurring at a time when there is an absence of activity, even though that activity occurs at a time when the relation [between the action and its result] has been destroyed by an inference that the action is a means to what is undesired (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*).

In this *nirukti*, due to the [undesired] connection, there would be the contingency of such usage occurring even in a state where the absence of the application of the prohibition exists; therefore, the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is used to indicate that even the knowledge having itself as its object must be subsumed by a knowledge of itself that is not co-temporal with its own destruction, specifically entered as those respective individual instances (*tattadvyakti*). Here, the first occurrence of the word "self" (*sva*) refers to those respective related entities that serve as the delimiters of the causality for engagement.
