The second occurrence of the word "self," however, refers to those respective individual instances of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, as previously explained. By this—

The resulting meaning is as follows: [the action] is produced by an inference which is generated by a knowledge of the cause (the reason) that is conveyed by the knowledge of the *liṅ* suffix and so forth, occurring at a time not simultaneous with the destruction of the relation that has been negated. Thus, even though the property of being an inference (*anumititva*) is not specifically included [in the definition], there is no fault. It is therefore established that the meaning of the *liṅ* suffix, in the form of a prohibition, connects with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*), namely "effort" (*kṛti*), through this relation.

Furthermore, the word *nañ* (the negative particle) is a restatement of the connection of its own meaning—namely, absence—with the meaning of the verbal suffix through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*); it serves to capture the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the actual *liṅ* suffix and so forth. Thus, everything is consistent.

Thus it is established that *bhāvanā*—which has synonyms such as *pravartanā*, *preraṇā*, and *vidhi*—is the meaning of the optative (*liṅ*) suffix and the like when they are not accompanied by the negative particle (*nañ*). However, when accompanied by that [negative particle], it has synonyms such as *nivartanā*, *nivāraṇā*, *niṣedha*, and *pratiṣedha*. And because it resides in the word itself, it is called "verbal *bhāvanā*" (*śābdī-bhāvanā*) in the Veda. The delimitors of those respective capacities are the property of being an optative (*liṅtva*) and the property of being a precative/imperative (*loṭtva*), but not the property of being a gerundive (*tavyatva*) and so forth; for these latter have the sense of "command" (*praiṣa*) and the like, according to the traditional rule: "The *kṛtya* suffixes are used in the senses of command, permission, and appropriate time."

Because there is no traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that [the optative suffix] has the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*). In the case of an object already known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the "impulsion" (*praiṣa*) residing in a person is an "exhortation" (*atisarga*), which is the freedom to act as one desires. However, in cases such as "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), since the object is not already established, the traditionalists hold that the suffix indicates an injunction (*vidhi*) by setting aside the sense of exhortation. Alternatively, the status of being a substitute for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so on is the delimiting factor of the power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), because it is what is actually heard.
This concludes the determination of the three components of the verbal productive operation (*śābdībhāvanā*).

And regarding this verbal productive energy (*śābdabhāvanā*), they maintain that it possesses three constituent parts (*aṃśatraya*), just like the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*). Among these, engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) constitute the "thing to be brought about" (*bhāvya*), because they are respectively prompted by injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*niṣedha*), and because they are connected to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, the knowledge of injunction and prohibition generated by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth constitutes the "instrument" (*karaṇa*), because it prompts that which is to be brought about. This is merely a figurative designation as an instrument; however, it does not enter into the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) as an instrument, because it is not itself a verbal object (*aśābdatvāt*).

Thus, the knowledge of praise (*prāśastya*) and dispraise (*aprāśastya*) constitutes, respectively, the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) for injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*niṣedha*). This too exists in reality alone, and does not enter into the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) within verbal cognition, precisely because it is non-verbal (*aśābdatva*). Furthermore, that praise and dispraise are conveyed through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) recited in proximity to their respective injunctions and prohibitions. [This concludes] the investigation into the nature of the praise and dispraise as conveyed by the *arthavādas*.

Now, what is this "praise" (prāśastya), or rather, what is "non-praise" (aprāśastya)? It cannot be the possession of qualities (guṇavattva) or the possession of defects (doṣavattva), because it is impossible to establish the very nature of "quality" and "defect" [in these contexts]. For instance, in such passages as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" (*vāyurvai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā*) or "Others are non-animals compared to cows and horses" (*apaśavo vā anye go'śvebhyaḥ*), the swiftness of Vāyu and so forth is not a "quality," nor is the state of being a "non-animal"—which is the absence of the excellence found in cows and horses—a "defect."

This is because that knowledge would be inconstant (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to what is delimited by engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), and thus would not be conducive to [action]; furthermore, since qualities such as being "quickest" (*kṣepiṣṭhatva*) are presented through denotative power (*śakti*) itself, it would result in the collapse of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding their being metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*). Nor [is it the meaning] in terms of being the generator of heaven, hell, and so forth, precisely because of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as "heaven."

If it is argued that [the Arthavāda] would otherwise be purposeless (*vaiyarthyāpatti*) once that [prohibition] is established, we reply: *prāśastya* (commendability) consists in being a means to a desired end greater than the suffering produced by the action; *aprāśastya* (non-commendability) consists in producing an undesired result greater than the pleasure produced by it. Thus, these two are logically established. For this meaning is not established by anything else, as the injunction (*vidhi*) implies only the status of being a means to a desired or undesired end.
This concludes the determination of the necessity of the knowledge of commendability and so forth derived from the Arthavādas.

For this very reason, wherever an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not recited, it is necessarily implied by the injunction itself. Nor should it be argued that such knowledge is useless for engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), because even in the absence of such knowledge, engagement and withdrawal do occur due to the force of past karma when there is intense passion or aversion toward immediate pleasure or pain; and conversely, even when such knowledge is present, engagement and withdrawal may fail to arise due to the force of past karma.

Even if such knowledge exists, it is established for all in both common worldly experience and the Veda that this knowledge functions as intense attraction and aversion—consisting of liking and disliking—because one generally observes in everyone an intense desire for an object of greater interest than the immediate pain produced by an action, and an intense aversion toward a pain greater than an immediate pleasure. However, due to the intensity of past karma (*prācīna-karma*), its absence may occur in some instances even when that knowledge is present, but not in all cases.

Therefore, in the absence of intense past karma, the knowledge of the aforementioned praise or blame produces intense attachment or aversion; thus, it is useful for engagement or withdrawal by way of that [production]. Nor should it be argued that, because the knowledge of praise or blame is useless for one who possesses liking or dislike spontaneously, it is therefore useless for all persons; for even if it is useless for all persons, its validity as an *arthavāda* (explanatory passage) is established simply by its being useful for a particular person.

Furthermore, although the recollection produced by a mantra is of no use for one who already possesses an inherently established recollection, it is nonetheless justified to postulate that such recollection brings about prosperity (*abhyudaya*) on the strength of the mantra's traditional recitation (*āmnāna*), just as one postulates that the excellence (*prāśastya*) indicated by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) brings about prosperity on the strength of that arthavāda’s recitation. And since such excellence is conveyed by the arthavādas only through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is no violation of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that [the arthavāda] is figurative.

And regarding that indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) in the case of a collection of words situated in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the indication may reside either in the entire collection of words or in a single word alone, while the other words serve to apprehend the intended meaning (*tātparya*); this is another matter.

As for the manner in which excellence (*prāśastya*) and so forth are construed, many hold that such excellence or lack of excellence is construed with the verbal productive force (*śābdabhāvanā*) through the relation of being the "procedure" (*itikartavyatātva*). Some, however, hold that it is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and so forth through the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*). But in reality, according to the method to be explained later, it should be construed like the meaning of another nominal stem (*subanta*), in accordance with the parsimony (*lāghava*) of postulating a single causal relationship.

Excellence (prāśastya) is construed with activity (pravṛtti) through the relation of being produced by an intense desire for a desired object, which is itself produced by a cognition having that excellence as its object; whereas non-excellence (aprāśastya) is construed with activity through the relation of being the counter-positive of an absence, which is prompted by an intense aversion for an undesired object, which is itself produced by a cognition having that non-excellence as its object.

Nor should it be argued that the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) are redundant because the superiority [of the result] in the primary fruit is already established by the explanatory passage concerning the primary rite (*pradhāna*) itself—namely, in comparison with the immediate suffering produced by the performance [of the rites]—since there is no difference between the fruit produced by the auxiliaries and the fruit produced by the primary rite, and because no superiority is possible regarding the benefit to the sacrifice (*kratūpakāra*). This is not so, because those passages are intended to make known the superiority of the primary fruit in comparison with the aggregate of immediate sufferings produced by each respective auxiliary.

Therefore, the path elucidated by the foundational texts is this: in explanatory passages (arthavādas) associated with injunctions, there is an indication (lakṣaṇā) of excellence consisting in the quality of producing a superior fruit; and in explanatory passages associated with prohibitions, there is an indication of non-excellence consisting in the quality of generating intense suffering.
This is a statement of the nature of excellence and non-excellence as conceived by [the author] himself.

In reality, however, in the case of explanatory passages (arthavādas) concerning permissions or injunctions, as well as in explanatory passages concerning prohibitions such as "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," it is impossible for there to be such a characterization of excellence (*prāśastya*) or lack of excellence (*aprāśastya*). For instance, in the passage "When the omentum has been offered, one may eat the food of the initiated," it is not possible to indicate that the result called satisfaction is superior to the undesirable consequence produced by the action; this is because an undesirable consequence, established by the prohibition itself, must necessarily be greater [than any benefit].

Since it is established in common worldly experience that the excessiveness [of pleasure] relative to the immediate suffering produced by an action exists, such knowledge would be useless for motivating activity if a prohibition were present; whereas [in the case of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup], relative to the pleasure produced by taking the *ṣoḍaśī*...

It is impossible to conceive that the suffering produced by it (the Śyena sacrifice) could be greater [than the suffering of the victim]. Furthermore, if the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the Śyena were to indicate that the transgression (*abhicāra*) is greater than the immediate suffering produced by the Śyena, then such knowledge would have no utility for motivating action (*pravṛtti*). Nor can it be shown that [the Śyena] produces a greater suffering than the hellish torments and the like resulting from its employment; for this is already understood from the explanatory passage regarding the prohibition "one must not kill," which indicates that [the Śyena] is greater than the transgression itself.

Therefore, in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning injunctions (*vidhi*), excellence (*prāśastya*)—consisting in the state of not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*)—is indicated (*lakṣyate*) as co-extensive (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*) with the delimitor of the enjoinedness (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*). And in explanatory passages concerning prohibitions (*niṣedha*), non-excellence (*aprāśastya*)—consisting in the state of being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānubandhitva*)—is [indicated] as co-extensive with the delimitor of the prohibitedness (*niṣedhyatāvacchedaka*). Here, regarding the undesirable...

Intensity (*balavattva*) consists in being the object of intense aversion (*utkaṭadveṣa*), and not in mere superiority. For even regarding a suffering that is inferior to heaven, an intense aversion may occasionally arise due to the force of past karma; for this very reason, one does not engage in sacrifices and the like at such times. And because an intense aversion may also arise regarding a pleasure that is inferior to hell due to the force of past karma, for this very reason one engages in malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and the like.

For this very reason, in the case of sacrifices and the like, the quality of not being followed by a powerful undesirable result (balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva) exists only occasionally due to the force of past meritorious karma, but not at all times. It is for this reason that the phrase "by way of co-occurrence with the delimitor of prescriptivity" (vidheyatāvacchedakasāmānādhikaraṇyena) intends to express its occurrence as non-pervasive over time (kālikāvyāpyavṛttitva).

Thus, in cases such as the eating of *kalañja*, the cognition that it is connected with a powerful undesirable consequence occurs only at certain times due to the force of virtuous karma. Therefore, even in those instances, the phrase "the delimiter of the prohibitedness" (*niṣedhyatāvacchedaka*) and so forth is used for the purpose of establishing that [the undesirable consequence] is temporally non-pervasive (*kālikāvyāpyavṛtti*). It is precisely for the sake of such a cognition of non-pervasive occurrence that the word "fitness" (*yogyatā*) is employed in the *Kaustubha* and other works.
This serves the purpose of the cognitions of commendability and non-commendability.

And such knowledge of the absence of a connection with a powerful undesirable consequence (balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvajñāna) serves, for that person by whom the sacrifice has always been perceived as being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence, to produce the cognition of invalidity regarding the [present] cognition of its occurrence.

For one who has always understood that the eating of *kalañja* is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), the knowledge of such a powerful undesirable consequence serves the purpose of producing a cognition of non-validity regarding the cognition of its occurrence (i.e., the eating). This is because a certainty of the absence of a property in a common locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*) stands in opposition to a cognition of the presence of that property under its delimiting condition (*avacchedakāvacchedena*). Consequently, the knowledge of such commendation (*prāśastya*) is useful for instigating action by way of providing the necessary causal conditions (*sāmagrī*).
And such knowledge of non-praiseworthiness is useful for desisting [from an action] by way of obstructing the causal complex for engagement (*pravṛtti-sāmagrī*).

This is possible in the case of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning a permissive injunction (*abhyanujñā-vidhi*), because it makes known that the eating of food by one consecrated (*dīkṣita*) after the offering of the omentum (*vapā-homa*) is not followed by an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭānanubandhitva*), which is the reason for the prohibition. Nor should it be argued that since this [non-praiseworthiness] consists in the absence of a defect (*doṣābhāva*), it is already implied by the injunction itself, making the explanatory passage redundant. For even if that is implied by the injunction, it is still appropriate for the explanatory passage to convey—through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—that it is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavad-aniṣṭānanubandhitva*).

Thus, even in the case of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) prohibiting the taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup, it is understood that "strength" (*balavatva*)—defined as being the object of intense aversion—is indicated through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with respect to even a slight, temporary suffering produced by the taking of the cup; therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
This is the manner of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) employed by the words of explanatory passages for the purposes of praise (*stuti*) and censure (*nindā*).

Therefore, in such instances of praise and censure—as in the passage beginning with "Vāyu is the swiftest"—the intended meaning is indicated solely through the relationship between the sentence-meaning and the sentence-meaning that has become the object of the verbal cognition produced by the knowledge of the literal sense of the *arthavāda* words. And that sentence-meaning is of this nature: "Vāyu, possessing qualities such as extreme swiftness, quickly bestows the fruit arising from the ritual for which he is the deity. For here, in order to avoid the redundancy of the particle *eva* in the phrase "sa eva" (he alone), the construction is to be understood as "he indeed causes [the fruit] to be attained."

Consequently, because indifference is thereby excluded, there arises the perception of speediness and other qualities in the act of giving. Furthermore, the verbal cognition produced is precisely that which is not the primary intended meaning (tātparya), just as the flow [of water] is presented by the word "Ganges. Since it is observed that the knowledge of speediness residing in the result generally generates an intensity of desire for that result, the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of praise is established through the existence of that relationship. This should be inferred in other cases as well. This is the manner in which praise is indicated through explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) having a secondary (*gauṇa*) meaning.

However, where there is a certainty of inappropriateness, such verbal comprehension does not occur; for example, in cases such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), because the relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*) is sublated. In that instance, the word "sacrificer" is accepted as being used figuratively (*gauṇa*) with respect to the grass-bundle, by virtue of its connection to the quality of performing a function similar to the function performed by the sacrificer. Thus, following the verbal comprehension produced by the sentence "The sacrificer is the grass-bundle," [the grass-bundle] is [designated as such] through its connection with the sentence-meaning, which consists in its being the performer of its own functions.

The definition of praise (*stuti*) consists in the state of not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). Nor should it be argued: "Why not accept a secondary sense (*gauṇī*) for the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) and, having accepted the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of 'not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence,' allow its connection with the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*)? For, in the case of the word *yajamāna* functioning as a praise residing in the *prastara*, there is no relationship between the primary meaning (*śakya*) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*). Furthermore, in our view, because there is no mutual connection between two words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), a connection with the *prastara* would be untenable. Nor is this so...

At the stage of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) that is not the intended meaning (*tātparya*), there is an impossibility of the connection of the object denoted by the secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*)—even though it is qualified by its capacity to perform its own function—with the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) through the relation of identity (*abheda*). This is because the connection between the two [the grass-bundle and the excellence] would be merely secondary (*pāriṣṭaka*), since both would connect only with the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*) supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*). Therefore, once the verbal cognition has been generated by the sentence containing the supplied verb, the excellence (*prāśastya*) indicated by that [verb] subsequently connects with the injunction (*vidhi*).

Nor can it be argued that even later on, one might simply take the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) as indirectly indicating (*lakṣaṇā*) something possessing excellence, and then—by accepting a mutual relationship obtained through subsequent syntactic connection (*pārṣṭhikānvaya*)—allow the meaning of the supplied verb (*ākhyāta*) itself to be connected to both [the sacrificer and the excellence], since the connection is already established by accepting a figurative indication (*gauṇī-garbhā lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of praise within the word "sacrificer" right from the beginning.

It should not be argued that there need be only a single verbal cognition (śābdabodha) and that the connection with the injunction (vidhi) is superfluous, since the fulfillment of its expectancy is possible through the unity of the sentence as a whole; for when it is possible to have a single sentence by accepting figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), a split of the sentence (vākyabheda) is improper. Nor can it be maintained that, even when the meaning of the supplied verb is connected according to our view, there is still the possibility of a single sentence—just as in the case of "Look, the deer runs"—by way of the meaning of one verb being construed as a qualifier (prakāra) of the meaning of the injunctive verb.

For fear of violating the grammatical rule that the meaning of the verb (ākhyāta) is the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*), if there were two verbs—as in the case of the mantra "syonaṃ te"—it would necessarily follow that they constitute distinct sentences. Otherwise, the bhāvanā of the subsidiaries such as the *prayāja* offerings would also connect with the principal bhāvanā by way of being a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), resulting in the undesirable consequence that everything would belong to a single sentence.

In expressions such as "Look, the deer runs," however, since the word "look" (*paśya*) does not produce a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) without an object, it is logical that the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of running is construed with it as its object. For there is no lack of completion of the verbal cognition without an object, as there would be without the connection of other *kārakas* (grammatical factors), because this would result in every sentence being inherently incomplete (*sākāṅkṣa*). Therefore, having accepted figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of excellence in the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) alone, if one were to accept its construction with the meaning of the supplied verb, it would lead to a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*); hence, figurative indication is accepted for the entire sentence.

In some cases, there is the acceptance of the position that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) form a single syntactical unit (*vākyaikavākyatā*) with injunctions (*vidhi*). However, in reality, when two finite verbs (*ākhyāta*) are present, the split of a sentence (*vākyabheda*) is not a defect; thus, there is no evidence for the figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) of the term "sentence" [to such a construction]. Consequently, in instances such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), there is no harm even if they form a single syntactical unit. Similarly, in cases such as "One should offer with wild sesame gruel," since there is no attainment of a single syntactical unit with the injunction for the milk-oblation through the figurative indication of excellence (*prāśastya-lakṣaṇā*), it results in being a separate sentence. This is because, in that case, the notion of a single syntactical unit is perceived through the word "or" (*vā*). The same applies to cases such as "He chooses one."

Since it is untenable for there to be separate sentences due to their being injunctive or because it would result in an option (*vikalpa*), one must accept the unity of the sentence even by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) regarding excellence (*prāśastya*) within the sentence, as there is no other way. For in that case, one does not accept *lakṣaṇā* in only a single word, as is done in the case of "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*).

The connection of the indicated excellence (*prāśastya*) with the meaning of the subsequent word is possible; therefore, in that case, the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs within the sentence itself. Consequently, where one accepts the indication of excellence in a single word and accepts its connection with the meanings of the other words so as to reach the completion of the sentence-meaning, there exists a syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*) between the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and the injunction (*vidhi*).

However, where it is not so, we consider it logical that in all such cases, having accepted the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of excellence (*prāśastya*) within the sentence itself, there is a syntactic unity of the injunctive injunction (*vidhi*) and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) because that which is presented as a word-meaning (*padārtha*) connects only with the meaning of the injunctive verb (*ākhyāta*). Thus, it is established that the verbal productive urge (*śābdībhāvanā*), denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, being assisted by the cognition of excellence and through the mediation of the implication of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), connects with the "activity" (*kṛti*) which is the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*)—the meaning of the verb.
Thus ends the section on Injunction (*vidhivāda*) in the *Bhaṭṭatantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Khaṇḍadeva.
Now follows the theory of *bhāvanā* by way of refuting the view that the meaning of the nominative case is the primary qualificand;
this is a restatement of the cognition held by the logicians (*tārkika*) in which the meaning of the nominative case is the primary qualificand.

Now, it may be argued that there is no evidence for the view that the *kṛti* (the effort or action), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), is the primary qualificandum (*mukhya-viśeṣya*). To explain: it is undisputed that the number—such as singularity and so on—denoted by the *tiṅ*-suffix is construed with Caitra or others, who are presented by a nominative word functioning as a qualifier of something else, through the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā*). And this [number] resides in Caitra in a sentence like "Caitra cooks rice" (*caitra odanaṃ pacati*), where the verbal suffix denotes the agent (*kartṛ-ākhyāta*); and it resides in the rice in a sentence like "Rice is cooked by Caitra" (*odanaḥ pacyate caitreṇa*), where the verbal suffix denotes the object (*karman-ākhyāta*), because in those cases that very [rice or Caitra] serves as a qualifier of something else.

Because the other [term] functions as a qualifier for properties such as being the object (*karman*), and because in examples such as "Maitra goes like Caitra," even though Caitra is presented by a word ending in the nominative suffix (*prathamā*), the number denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) does not apply to him; this is because he serves as a qualifier of the similarity—which is the meaning of the word *iva*—through the relation of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*). Rather, the number applies only to Maitra. For this very reason, in cases such as "The face is like the moon" and "The moon shines," the number applies to both.

Because in both cases [the agent and the object], there is the property of being presented by a word that is not a qualifier of anything else. In the case of a verb expressing existence (*bhāvākhyāta*), since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not a qualifier of anything else, the term "ending in the nominative" (*prathamānta*) is used to exclude the occurrence of number (*saṃkhyā*) in that context. Consequently, just like that [agent], the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verb also has its syntactic relation (*anvaya*) to that very [nominative] through the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā*), but it does not have the status of being the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*). If it is argued that this is because of parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating a single causal relationship—namely, that the presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative of the aforementioned type is the cause for a verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) characterized by having as its qualifier a meaning of the verb other than time and so forth—then [we reply]: [This is not so,] because... (The argument continues with the refutation of the proposed causal model).

The presentation of the fact that the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is [the agent] by way of the exclusion of that [other view] is [untenable], because it is possible for the meaning of the nominative case-ending (the first-case suffix), as stated above, to be related to the action (*kṛti*) through the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatā*), just like time and other factors; thus, there is no restrictive factor for postulating such a causal relationship [where the action is the locus]. Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that serves as a restrictive factor for the understanding that the cultivation denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) must necessarily be construed as a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the meaning of the nominative case-ending.

For an experience that contradicts the experiences of Jaimini, Pāṇini, and others must be determined by means of an oath; this is because Jaimini, in the sūtra *tadbhūtānāṃ kriyārthena samāmnāyaḥ*, stated that there is an experience in which the action (*kriyā*) is the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyaka*). Furthermore, such an experience does not exist for Gautama either, since he maintains that the number expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) cannot be construed with the meaning of a nominal stem (*nāman*).

Furthermore, even the number expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) does not indeed undergo syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the referent of a noun, such as Caitra, because that would contradict the number already expressed by the nominative case-ending. Nor can it be argued that this [verbal number] lacks obstructive power because its purpose is merely grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), for it is more appropriate that the number expressed by the verbal suffix—which is presented immediately due to the proximity of being contained within the same word—should serve the purpose of grammatical correctness, rather than the number presented with delay [by the nominal suffix]. And it is not the case that, under such a view, there would be the undesirable consequence of failing to experience the cognition of duality in the sentence "Caitra and Maitra go" (*caitro maitraśca gacchataḥ*).

Just as there is an experience of the concomitance of duality [with the verb], it is impossible to deny the experience of the concomitance of the singularity of each [object] with the case-suffix (*sup*); therefore, since one of these experiences must necessarily be admitted as non-verbal, it is more appropriate that the number belongs to the duality expressed by another word. As for the demonstration of the concomitance of number with the agent (the *kartṛ*) denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), although the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) has a primary denotative power (*śakti*) toward the action (*kṛti*) due to parsimony, it is nonetheless necessary—according to the method to be explained—that the agent and so forth appear through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā*). And in that case, because the number conjoins through the proximity of being expressed by the same word, its concomitance never occurs with the nominative ending (*prathamā-anta*).

Therefore, by the maxim that "those denoted by a single word have a single qualificand as their default state," and in accordance with the parsimony of postulating a single causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), if one maintains the view that the connection of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is with the number as the qualificand, then both [the agent and the number] connect with the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, which are themselves indicated (*lakṣya*) by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). They do not, however, connect with that which is presented by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*). We shall explain later how, this being the case, the productive urge possesses the status of the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*) with respect to that [agent].
Having extracted the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), we shall demonstrate the untenability [of that view] therein.

Furthermore, in your system, the causal relation is established as follows: with respect to a verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*)—qualified by being produced by the knowledge of a verbal suffix (*ākhyātapada*) and characterized by a subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of the suffix (which is distinct from time and so forth)—there exists a cause qualified by being an apprehension (*upasthiti*) whose qualificandum is an object not already qualified by another, which is produced by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntapada*) and related to it by the relation of subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*). However, this [causal relation] is not possible.

In sentences such as "Caitra does not cook," "Caitra cooks indeed," and "Caitra also cooks," there would be the undesirable consequence that the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), would only be construed with Caitra himself. Consequently, it could not be construed with the negation (*nañ*) in the sense of non-existence, nor with the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyāvṛtti*)—which is a part of the meaning of the particle "indeed" (*evakāra*)—nor with the conjunction (*samuccaya*) which constitutes the meaning of the word "also" (*api*). In those cases, since number (*saṃkhyā*) is construed with Caitra, it follows that number must be construed with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the *bhāvanā*. It is stated that even if the qualification "not being co-uttered with particles" (*nipātāsamabhivyāhṛtatva*) were added to the aforementioned causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), this would still result in no simplification; rather, it would lead to a lack of uniformity (*ananugama*) and excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Thus it is explained.

Furthermore, this is because the restriction [of the rule] would also result in over-extension (*vyabhicāra*). For this very reason, "being co-uttered with a particle" (*nipāta-samabhivyāhṛtatvam*) is not a qualifier of "the verbal suffix" (*ākhyāta*). This is because the number (*saṃkhyā*) could not then be construed with Caitra. Nor can it be argued that, even with that qualifier, one might accept a separate causal relationship between the number and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) in cases where they are co-uttered with a particle, thereby accounting for their respective construals with their own substrata;
for in our own system, we have stated the parsimony (*lāghava*) in that regard.

[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate numerous relations of cause and effect (*anekakāryakāraṇabhāva*). In our view, however, because all [words] are connected with the *bhāvanā* through a single relation of cause and effect—in the manner that will be explained later—and because the *bhāvanā* is the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*), that [consequence] does not arise. Furthermore, there is no uniformity even across all particles (*nipāta*), since in cases such as "Caitra alone cooks" (*caitra eva pacati*) or "A jar alone is seen" (*ghaṭa eva dṛśyate*), a connection is perceived when they are used in conjunction with a verb.

Furthermore, it is not possible to maintain the restriction that dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) between number and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) occurs only in cases where [the verb] is uttered in conjunction with an action (*kriyā*), and not elsewhere; for in examples such as *pacati na caitraḥ* ("Caitra does not cook") and *caitro na pacati* ("Caitra does not cook"), dissimilarity exists in both ways. Therefore, according to your view, because the relation of cause and effect would be infinite and because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), that which is presented by a word ending in the nominative case cannot be the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the productive urge. This is the specific reasoning regarding the primary qualificandhood of the productive urge.

Furthermore, in the case of "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), since there is no word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntapada*), a cognition having the *bhāvanā* as its qualifier cannot arise due to the absence of the necessary cause. Therefore, given the other causal factors, there is no obstacle to the *bhāvanā* being the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*). Nor should it be argued that, in accordance with experience, one should postulate that the knowledge of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapada*) is the cause specifically for a cognition qualified by having the *bhāvanā* as its qualifier, and thus assume an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a nominative word to account for such a cognition; for experience is something that can only be determined through an oath.

Because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate a causal relationship between those two. Nor does this entail for you the undesirable consequence that in expressions such as "Caitra is wise," where there is no verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the nominative-terminated word would become the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*). This is because the cognition of a nominal suffix (*sup*) is a cause only with respect to a cognition whose content is qualified by the meaning of a nominal suffix; furthermore, according to the method to be explained, even the nominative case possesses an object other than number (*saṃkhyā*).

Even in the case of non-remnant (anatiritta) food, there is no need to postulate that the knowledge of a word ending in the nominative case is the cause for a cognition characterized by having as its qualifier an object presented by a word ending in the nominative case; thus, the supply of a verb (*ākhyāta*) is justified in such instances. Nor is there a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), because such [supply] is not a fault since it is sanctioned by traditional Smṛti; furthermore, even in the absence of the knowledge of the grammatical rule—"the verb *as* (to be), in the third person, is understood even when not explicitly used"—such a cognition is accepted.

Furthermore, if the knowledge of the verb *ākhyāta* (the verbal suffix) is held to be the cause for a cognition delimited by the property of being a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is the sense of the verbal root (*bhāvanā*), then in cases of the impersonal (*bhāva*) *ākhyāta* such as "Caitra sleeps" (*caitreṇa supyate*) or "The sky stands" (*gaganena sthīyate*), there would be the undesirable consequence of having to supply a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamā*). If, on the other hand, one accepts that in those instances the cognition has the meaning of the *ākhyāta* itself as its primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and one introduces the condition of being "distinct from the impersonal sense" (*bhāvabhinnatva*) into the delimiting factor of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), then even that involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). In our view, however, since in all cases the cognition has the meaning of the *ākhyāta* as its primary qualificand, this does not apply even in the case of the impersonal *ākhyāta*.

Because the agent is not denoted [by the verb], the nominative case ending (*prathamā*) would fail to apply. Furthermore, if the connection between the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) and number were with a nominative-terminated word that is not a qualifier of anything else, then in cases such as *caitra eva pacati* ("Caitra alone cooks") or *ghaṭa eva dṛśyate* ("Only a jar is seen"), where would the connection of the productive operation and number occur, or how would verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) arise? It cannot be in Caitra and so forth; for the productive operation would have to connect to the exclusion of non-connection (*anyayogavyāvṛtti*), which is a part of the meaning of the particle *eva*, by way of the relation of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitākatva*) of the difference, and the number would have to connect to the "other" (the excluded object) which is also a part of the meaning of *eva*, by way of the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā*). [This is untenable.]

This is because those two [words] lack the status of being presented by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*). Nor can it be argued that even for indeclinables (*avyaya*), there is no contradiction in their being nominative due to the elision of the case-suffix (*sup-lopa*), as in the example "curd remains" (*dadhi tiṣṭhati*);
for even if that were the case, we observe the use of the singular number in expressions such as "Caitra alone cooks" (*caitra eva pacati*).

For this very reason, the following view is rejected: that by accepting a double connection through the diversity of the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *pacati*, there arises a verbal cognition whose qualificand is a portion of the meaning of the particle *eva*—namely, "one distinct from Caitra who possesses an activity conducive to cooking, and [Caitra] who is the locus of the absence of an activity conducive to cooking. This is because, due to the plurality of such [entities], the singular number cannot be construed with them; furthermore, since Caitra functions as a qualifier of another [the absence], he likewise cannot be the locus of that [connection].

Furthermore, the word *caitra* cannot convey its meaning twice—once as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and once as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Consequently, the resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) would be: "one who is other than Caitra possesses an absence of an effort conducive to cooking. Moreover, "not being a qualifier of another" must be defined as the absence of that which is a qualifier, qualified by the absence of being a qualificand. Even if this were the case, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that dual and plural numbers would apply even in cases such as "Caitra and Maitra go," just as they do in "Caitra, Maitra, and others go."

Furthermore, the use of the singular number [in the verb] is not justified in the same way as in the case of the sentence "Caitra goes, but Maitra does not. For if that were the case, just as in that instance the word "goes" is supplied [to both], resulting in two distinct sentences, so too here there would result two distinct sentences due to the difference between the primary subjects (*mukhya-viśeṣya*). In our view, however, the cognition is: "the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) residing in Caitra and residing in one other than Caitra has a single agent. And the relation to Caitra as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*) regarding the difference is obtained through syntactic implication (*pārṭhika*). Alternatively, the particle *eva* itself bears the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) there; thus, there is no contradiction. This is because the status of the efficient force as the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) is established by experience.

In reality, however, when the question "What are Caitra and Maitra doing? is asked regarding the sentence "Caitra cooks and Maitra does not cook," the answer "Caitra alone cooks" would result [if the subject were the primary qualificand]. For this very reason, it has been stated that there is no cognition where the first-case-inflected noun is the primary qualificand, because the answer "He cooks" would result when the question "What is Caitra doing? is asked. Therefore, the fact that the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is the primary qualificand is established by experience itself.
Thus ends the *Bhāvanāvāda* in the *Bhaṭṭatantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Khaṇḍadeva.
Now, regarding the investigation into the non-causative nature of the nominative (*prathamā*):

furthermore, even if it were granted that the aforementioned cognition produced by a word ending in the nominative case is a cause—by virtue of being common to both number and *bhāvanā*—in your own view, the nominative...

What is the motivating factor for the third case (instrumental) and the others? It cannot be the expression or non-expression of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth as the motivators, because you do not accept that [the verbal suffixes express the agent]. Nor can it be the expression or non-expression of number (*saṃkhyā*), because since number is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) everywhere, the nominative (*prathamā*) would apply in all instances, resulting in the undesirable consequence that the second case (*dvitīyā*) and other cases would never occur. If, on the other hand, the motivating factor for the nominative is simply being coreferential with the number conveyed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*);

And its connection [is as follows]: when there is co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, it resides in the object (*karman*), which is the locus of the result known as the object of volition (*kṛti-viṣayatva*); when there is co-utterance with verbal suffixes such as *śap*, it resides in the agent (*kartṛ*), which is the locus of volition. In whatever kind of co-utterance the agent is expressed by the verb according to the Grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) view, or the agent is indicated (*lakṣaka*) according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, in that same kind of co-utterance, the number conveyed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) belongs to the agent in the form of the locus of volition.

In whatever co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra) those two [the verb and the noun] are considered to have the status of denoting the object (*karman*), in that same co-occurrence, the number conveyed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) resides in the object in the form of the content of the volition (*kṛti*). Therefore, it is precisely the non-denotation of such a number that serves as the cause for the use of the nominative case (*prathamā*) following a noun that expresses the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of that number. Conversely, the non-denotation of such a number serves as the cause for the use of the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*), accusative (*dvitīyā*), and other case-endings following a noun that does not express its qualificand, but rather denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and so forth.

If it is argued that for this very reason, in the case of a verb expressing existence (*bhāvākhyāta*), because the number residing in the agent or the object is not denoted, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs—as in "caitreṇa supyate" (it is slept by Caitra)—and in the case of a verb expressing the object (*karmākhyāta*), as in "caitreṇa pacyate odanaḥ" (rice is cooked by Caitra), the nominative (*prathamā*) occurs only on the word denoting the object; whereas in the case of a verb expressing the agent (*kartṛākhyāta*), as in "caitraḥ pacati" (Caitra cooks), it occurs only on the word denoting the agent—thus a systematic rule (*vyavasthā*) is obtained.

If that were the case, there would arise the undesirable consequence of such usages as *caitreṇa pācakasya putraḥ* ("the son of the cooker by Caitra") or *odanaḥ pakvasya viklṛttiḥ* ("the softening of the cooked rice"), because the number residing in the agent or the object is not expressed by the *kṛt*-suffix. Furthermore, there would be no occurrence of such usages as *caitrasya pācakasya putraḥ* ("the son of Caitra, who is a cooker") or *odanasya viklṛttiḥ* ("the softening of the rice"). As it is said: "Even a poison-tree, having been nurtured, is not fit to be cut down by oneself."

Furthermore, in such cases as these, the occurrence of the nominative case (*prathamā*) would also result [undesirably]. Nor can it be argued that the nominative is established there simply because the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth are expressed by the *kṛt* suffix or the indeclinable (*nipāta*), and that the meaning of the rule is that the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and others occur when neither number nor the agent and so forth are expressed. Even if that were the case, the nominative would still not be obtained for Caitra in examples such as "Maitra goes like Caitra," because the number residing in Caitra and the agency residing in Caitra are not expressed by the finite verb ending (*tiṅ*) in "goes."

As for the view that "the third case-ending occurs when the efficient force (*kṛti*) is not denoted, the second case-ending when the result (*phala*) is not denoted, but when [either] is denoted, the first case-ending occurs everywhere"—that too is incorrect. For in the impersonal construction (*bhāvākhyāta*), since the efficient force is denoted, the first case-ending would result. Furthermore, even in the transitive construction (*karmākhyāta*), because it is glossed as "it is done" (*kriyate*), the denotation of the efficient force is necessary, and thus the first case-ending would again result. In our own view, however, although the *tiṅ* suffix denotes the efficient force, the agent and so forth are also denoted through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) according to the method to be explained later, just as they are by the *kṛt* suffixes.

By means of the indeclinable *sāmpratam*, which signifies "fitting" (*yogya*), the agent and other factors are denoted; thus, the occurrence of the nominative case is justified everywhere. Even in expressions such as *caitra iva* ("like Caitra"), there is the denotation of the agent because the word *iva* denotes a similarity consisting in the status of being the agent of the act of going. Likewise, in expressions such as *candra iva mukham* ("the face is like the moon"), since the verb "is" (*asti*) must necessarily be supplied, there is the denotation of the agent in the form of being the locus of existence delimited by the quality of being delightful.

For this very reason, since the *ktvā* suffix also expresses the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), the use of the nominative case is justified even for the first instance of the word "Caitra" in the sentence, "Having cooked, Caitra eats" (*caitraḥ paktvā caitro bhuṅkte*). It should not be argued that, in a construction such as "Having been cooked by Caitra, [it] is eaten by Caitra" (*caitreṇa paktvā caitreṇa bhujyate*), the nominative would be improper for the first "Caitra" because the agent has already been expressed by the *ktvā* suffix. For in that case, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) signifies the instrument (*karaṇatva*), as in examples such as "You know yourself by yourself" (*ātmānam ātmanā vetsi*) or "Having entered with this living self, let me manifest names and forms" (*anena jīvenā'tmanā'nupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi*). Thus, the third case is used there to denote the instrumental role.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*: "That which is expressed by a word through its own function (*vṛtti*) as a factor (*kāraka*) whose action is conveyed by that same word with which it is syntactically connected—that is the state of being 'expressed' (*abhihitatva*) which serves as the cause for the use of the nominative case. And this [state] exists in examples such as *caitraḥ pacati* ("Caitra cooks") and *odanaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is cooked"), because [in these cases] there is agency, objecthood, and so forth, residing in Caitra and the others.

Because it is expressed by a word denoting an action that lacks a specific agent (*niruktakriyāpada*). And in cases such as "the cook goes" (*pācakena gamyate*), the person conveyed by the *kṛt* suffix is construed only with the action of going, not with the action of cooking; for that [action of going] is the very first to be construed with him. Furthermore, "construal" (*anvaya*) here is intended to mean precisely that which becomes the object of the initial verbal cognition. By this—

In such cases as “The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of *udumbara* wood” and “One desiring heaven should sacrifice,” although the sacrificial post, heaven, and so forth are indicated by the nominative case as having the character of an object (*karman*) and the like, the nominative case is justified because agency (*kartṛtva*) has been expressed in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), which consists in [the post’s] being the locus of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) whose agent is the primary [post]. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this; for if that were the case, since there would be no awareness of the futility [of the sentence] due to the absence of knowledge of its religious merit (*dharma*), there would be no indication of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*), and consequently, the assumption of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would be untenable.

For this very reason, in cases where indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs solely due to the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*), the verbal cognition produced by indication is necessarily the first to arise; and since the agenthood has not yet been established therein, the word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntapada*) would indeed be semantically incompatible. For example, in the sense "Caitra exerts himself toward cooking by means of fire," one might say "Fire and Caitra exert themselves toward cooking. Here, the verbal cognition arises through the indication of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) for the nominative case. Indeed, in this instance, the indication of instrumentality occurs precisely because of the impossibility of syntactic connection. Therefore, in that case, [the cognition] proceeds from indication.

Since there was no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) previously, this very cognition must be stated as the first [cognition]. Nor is the agency (*kāraṇatva*) manifesting at that time expressed by the word *yatate*, which conveys the action connected with itself (i.e., the effort). As for the agency expressed by *yatate*, that does not reside in fire; thus, due to the absence of the form that serves as the cause for the nominative case, that sentence is ungrammatical (*asādhu*) in that sense. Since the aforementioned type of agency residing in that [fire] is not denoted by the verbal suffix of the object (*karmākhyāta*), the use of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) there is indeed appropriate.

Thus, in the case of "caitreṇa bhuktvā gamyate" (having eaten, Caitra goes), since Caitra’s connection to the act of eating is absent, the use of the instrumental case is justified by accepting his connection to the act of going. And so, in cases such as "paktvaudano bhujyate" (having cooked, rice is eaten), when there is an expectancy for an object (*karman*) for the root *pac*, the sentence is completed by supplying the word "odana" in the accusative case. For there is no authoritative evidence for a rule stating that a *kāraka* which has been assigned to a primary action must also be assigned to a subordinate action, on account of which one would have to supply [the term] through ellipsis.

Even without an explicit sentence, [the meaning] would be complete. If that were the case, then in instances such as "Having eaten rice, the scripture is studied" (*odanaṃ bhuktvā śāstraṃ paṭhyate*) or "Even having heard the meaning, it was not accepted by that evil-minded person" (*śrutvāpyarthaṃ nānumataḥ stena so'rthaḥ kubuddhinā*), the use of the accusative case would be untenable. Therefore, in cases where the suffix *ktvā* follows a transitive root, even when there is an ellipsis of the word *odanam* (rice) ending in the accusative, the verbal cognition is established even without a word denoting a specific agent; thus, there is no obstacle to the usage "Having eaten, Caitra goes" (*caitreṇa bhuktvā gamyate*).

If, however, it is considered that under this view there would be the undesirable consequence of such usages as *caitro bhuktvā* (having eaten, Caitra goes) and *caitreṇa gamyate* (Caitra is being gone by), then let the suffix *ktvā* not have the expressive power (*śakti*) for both "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) and "priority of time" (*pūrvakālatva*). Rather, because it is a *kṛt* suffix denoting an action (*bhāva*), it denotes the action itself; its connection with the subsequent action occurs through the relations of having the same agent and priority of time. [This concludes] the determination of the factors necessitating the use of the vocative case.

And this [occurrence] is in a domain where there is no cognition [of the agent]; for the vocative case is independently the subject of predication (*vidheya*). For this very reason, even when the agency (*kartṛtva*) residing therein is not expressed, the usage *caitra maitraḥ pacati* ("O Caitra, Maitra cooks") is possible. And thus, the expression *caitraḥ paktvā caitro bhuṅkte* ("Caitra, having cooked, eats") is indeed an incorrect usage, because the agent-factor (*kartṛ-kāraka*) that has occurred in relation to the primary action [is not coreferential with the subsequent action].

Alternatively, its grammatical correctness may be maintained by accepting the rule that the suffix *ktvā* occurs even when the action is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). Or rather, it should be understood that while the verb expressing the principal action takes the active voice (*kartṛ-ākhyāta*), the suffix *ktvā* also functions through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in cases such as shared agency (*samānakartṛkatva*). For this very reason, the construction "caitreṇa paktvā caitro bhuṅkte" (Having cooked by Caitra, Caitra eats) is also ungrammatical. For this same reason, in the sentence "mayaiva paktvā mayaiva bhujyate" (By me alone having cooked, it is eaten by me alone), the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs precisely in reference to the agent.

In expressions such as *paktvaudano bhujyate* ("Having cooked, rice is eaten"), there is indeed the ellipsis of the object (*karman*) as a *kāraka*; likewise, usages such as *odanaṃ bhuktvā śāstraṃ paṭhyate* ("Having eaten rice, the scripture is studied") are easily accounted for. Similarly, in cases such as *pacanī sthālī* ("the cooking pot"), *dānīyo brāhmaṇaḥ* ("the Brāhmaṇa worthy of a gift"), and *kuṭhāraḥ karaṇam* ("the axe is the instrument"), the occurrence of the nominative case is justified because the status of locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) and so forth is expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix. Nor does this [explanation] fail even where, following a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), there are forms such as *pacatitarām*, *pacatikalpam*, *pacataḥ kalpam*, or *pacantikalpam*, which express excellence (*atiśaya*) or slightness (*īṣad*).

Alternatively, it may be argued that the suffix is used in the sense of completion (*samāpti*); however, since it is a *taddhita* suffix, it receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, when there is a desire to express only the meaning of the nominal stem, it ends in the nominative case. Thus, in that instance, the form that would trigger the nominative case is absent, because the agency (*kartṛtva*) residing in that [suffix] is not expressed by a finite verb (*tiṅ*). This is because the locus of "slightness" (*īṣattva*) and so forth connects only with the verbal process of cooking (*pākabhāvanā*) through a relation of difference (*bhedasambandha*). To this it must be replied: in such cases, we accept that the primary meaning of the verbal root itself (*dhātu*) indicates "slight incompleteness" and the like through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

Since it is accepted that the definition [of a noun] serves to indicate the intended meaning of the suffix *kab* and so forth, the coreferential connection (*anvaya*) with that meaning is not accepted; therefore, the nominative case (*prathamā*) used therein has the purpose of mere grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*). For this very reason, this [rule regarding gender and number] is the motivator (*prayojaka*) only for that nominative which generates verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), and not for that which exists for the sake of grammatical correctness. As for the latter, there is simply no reason to bypass the nominative case.

However, some maintain that the non-expression [of the agent] by means of *kṛt* suffixes and the like is precisely the cause for the employment of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and other case-endings. It should be stated that the logical connection (*anvaya*) is possible even for wood and other such [instruments]. Precisely out of fear of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of such usage, I too have formulated the following restrictive rule: "For words expressing a *kāraka* denoted by a *kṛt*-suffix etc. which expresses its own meaning, the condition for the connection with the action of the non-different nominal meaning (or its gender and number) is that it must be mediated by an object presented by a case-suffix such as the accusative (*dvitīyā*), distinct from the gender and number presented by the nominal suffix (*sup*). In this context, the word "its own" (*sva*) refers to the action with which it is connected.

In this context, the phrase ending with "distinct" (*bhinnā*) is used because even a name-meaning (*nāmārtha*), such as Caitra, is directly construed with the action in expressions like *pacati* ("he cooks"). Furthermore, in cases such as *pācakam ānaya* ("bring the cook"), although the word *pācaka* denotes an agent expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix, its construction with the effort conducive to bringing necessarily requires that the status of being an object (*karmatva*), which is presented by the accusative case-ending, serves as the medium; hence the expression "denoting itself" (*svabodhaka*).

Since it will be explained later that even in cases such as *pācakaḥ pākam* ("the cooker [cooks] the cooking"), there is an understanding of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the instrumental case and others are necessary there to convey the causality and so forth of the firewood and other factors when they are construed with it. For this very reason, in accordance with this rule, the *Kaustubha* and other works do not accept the direct connection of the nominal stem meaning (*prātipadikārtha*) with the productive operation, nor its connection with the gender and number expressed by the case endings. Therefore, they say that in expressions such as *pacatikalpam*, the nominative case occurs when only the nominal stem meaning is intended to be expressed. This concludes the refutation of the superior view.

That is not so; for even in this case, since the suffix *kalpa* expresses a slight incompleteness (*īṣadasamāpti*), there would be the unavoidable consequence of a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) arising from the intended expression of a relationship of difference between that [incompleteness] and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, since even "slight incompleteness" is the meaning of such a nominal stem (*nāmārtha*), its connection with the aforementioned action would lack the mediation of the meaning of a second-case suffix (*dvitīyā*) or other such cases, which would result in a violation of the rule.

Therefore, we consider it correct to hold that although grammar elsewhere teaches the actual function (*vṛtti*) [of words], in the present instance it is intended merely to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).
