Thus ends the investigation into the factors necessitating the nominative case in the *Bhāṭṭatantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Khaṇḍadeva. Now begins the discussion on the definition of the agent (*kartṛ*).
Regarding the statement of the proof for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denoting the agent:

if it is argued that this [denotation] would be established only for one who maintains that the verbal suffix expresses *kṛti* (effort), yet there is no proof for that very point—[we reply: the question "What kind [of thing] is it? when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is uttered, is itself the proof in that regard. For a question concerning a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) is not possible without prior knowledge of the substratum (*dharmin*). Nor is such knowledge of the substratum possible according to your view, because [on your view] the cognition produced is only an indivisible sentence-meaning (*akhaṇḍavākyārtha*) whose qualificandum is the meaning of the verbal suffix and whose qualifier is the cooking—the meaning of the word *pacati*—related by the relation of *anukūlatā* (conduciveness).

Because, in the absence of the causal factor consisting of the cognitive presentation (upasthiti) generated by a word ending in the nominative case, it is impossible to produce a cognition in which the locus (āśraya) is the qualificandum and the effort (kṛti) is the qualifier. Although, in your view, there is also causality toward a cognition where effort is the qualifier based on the cognition of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), nevertheless, if that which delimits its effectness (kāryatāvacchedaka) is...

If [the nature of the cognition] is being a cognition whose qualifier is *kṛti* (effort), then, due to the absence of knowledge of the locus (*āśraya*), the absence of knowledge of the subject (*dharmin*) is indeed easily established. If, however, it is being a cognition whose qualificand is the locus and whose qualifier is *kṛti*, even then, since the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in the nominative case is a cause [of that cognition] in combination—just like a staff, a wheel, and so forth—their absence makes the non-arising [of the cognition] easy to establish.

Therefore, for the sake of providing the knowledge of the subject that justifies the question, and for the sake of supplying a word ending in the nominative case, the knowledge of the locus must necessarily be stated.

Regarding this, there is disagreement as to whether it is verbal (*śābda*), mental (*mānasa*), or a memory (*smaraṇa*). Among these, it is strictly verbal because of the grammatical rule: "The *l*-suffixes [denote] the object and the agent, and after intransitive verbs, they denote the state (*bhāva*). Here, by the word "and" (*ca*) in that rule, the term "agent" (*kartari*) from the preceding sūtra "kṛt suffixes denote the agent" is drawn forward; thus, the *l*-suffixes are obtained as denoting the agent as well. This is not intended to mean that the *l*-suffixes possess a primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the agent and so forth. For it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to assume a distinct intention (*tātparya*) for each individual word-meaning and its respective function.

Furthermore, since the agent has been determined to be denoted by the suffix through parsimony, the grammatical rule (Pāṇini 3.4.67) governing that suffix must be explained as employing only conventional indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*). Moreover, if the agent were merely mental, the connection of number with it would be untenable; additionally, upon hearing only the word *pacati*, there would arise the doubt as to whether the singularity pertains to the agent. This is also because the meaning of the primary suffix (*kṛt*) is explained as "the cooker" (*pācaka*) in the form *pacati* = *pācakaḥ*. Therefore, it is stated that the cognition of the substratum (the agent) is verbal. This concludes the demonstration of parsimony regarding the verbal nature of the agent.

And this is appropriate: for the sake of simplicity in postulating that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the cause of a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the number conveyed by the suffix—since the verbal suffix is more proximate than a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntapada*)—therefore, due to parsimony, the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*), and the requirement of the knowledge of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*), the verbal suffix has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth. By this, the view of those who maintain that the agent appears as a relational element (*saṃsargavidhayā*) is refuted; for in our system, singularity and the like are connected to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) precisely through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) residing in the agent and so forth, which are themselves the relational objects (*sāṃsargikaviṣaya*).

Thus, the claim that "cognition [of the meaning] occurs through that [denotation] alone" is refuted. For there is no inconsistency in the definition [of lakṣaṇā], since the doubt—"Is the agent of cooking one or many?"—cannot be dispelled by the word *pacati* (he cooks) [if it were taken only in its primary sense], and because it would otherwise result in the futility of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*). Furthermore, such a doubt would not even arise, as there is no cognition of the subject (*dharmin*) as qualified by its delimiting property (*dharmitāvacchedaka*). Nor is there any evidence for the claim that if a verbal cognition produced solely by denotative power (*śakti*) never occurs anywhere, it would be impossible for that very word to indicate another meaning (*lakṣaka*).

Because, just as the primary meaning is impossible, the cognition of another meaning is also untenable [otherwise], and thus indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—aided by the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghava*)—serves to grasp the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Even in that case, indication occurs according to a fixed rule: in instances where the verbal suffixes are *śap* and so on, it refers to the agent (*kartṛ*), and in instances where they are *yaṅ* and so on, it refers to the object (*karman*). The delimitor of the indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is either the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) or agency (*kartṛtva*), objecthood (*karmatva*), and so forth, or else an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).
[The following is] the proof that agency and the rest are indivisible adjuncts.

For agency and the like are indeed indivisible properties (*akhaṇḍadharma*) that are co-extensive with being the locus of volitional effort (*kṛti*) and so forth, as evidenced by the uniform linguistic usage; they are not, however, merely the state of being the locus of volitional effort. If that were the case, in the sentence "cooking is performed by Caitra" (*caitreṇa pākaḥ kriyate*), the meaning "cooking is to be accomplished by the volitional effort residing in Caitra" would be established by the expression "cooking by Caitra" (*caitreṇa pākaḥ*) alone. Consequently, the further employment of the word expressing volitional effort, namely "is performed" (*kriyate*), would result in redundancy. Therefore, agency and the like, as indivisible properties, are the actual meaning of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth.

And just as [the self] is the substratum (*āśraya*) and so forth, by postulating properties such as being defined by the effort (*kṛti*) and so on, the comprehension of the meaning—"The cooking is to be accomplished by an effort that defines the agency residing in Caitra"—is established. This has been stated according to the view of others; for in our own view, it will be explained later that the verbal cognition is simply that "the state of being to be accomplished by the aforementioned effort resides in the cooking. In any case, agency and the like are indivisible adjuncts (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).

This is accepted by the ancients for the purpose of establishing that the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the two [the husband and wife] resides in them collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), and for the purpose of establishing that the divinity (*devatātva*) of Agni and Soma resides in them collectively. Otherwise, since agency—defined as being the substratum of the verbal suffix (*kṛt*)—and divinity—defined as being the intended object of the substance being abandoned—would be distinct due to the difference in their substrata, the established doctrine of collective residence would be untenable. Therefore, taking agency and objecthood (*karmatva*) as the delimiters of the indicated property (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the agent and the object.
And this has been stated following the general rule.

In cases such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), where husband and wife have joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*) and the agenthood is characterized by a single grammatical number—where, according to the principle stated regarding the genitive case, there exists another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) apprehending a plurality of substrata, as in the case of husband and wife—the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) does not indicate the substratum through indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is because it would result in the non-connection of the singular number. Therefore, since there is no evidence for indicating duality, the agenthood itself is indicated by the verbal suffix through the property of agenthood (*kartṛtva-tvena*), rather than its substratum as well, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*).

For its cognition arises from the very sense [of the word] itself. And it is accepted that the cognition of agency occurs through the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth by means of the property of being an agent (*kartṛtva*). The only difference is this: in that case [the third case], it is by way of *śakti* (direct denotation), whereas here it is by way of *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Furthermore, in that very case, the coreferential connection (*anvaya*) with singularity is through a direct relation; it is not with the substratum (*āśraya*), because that [substratum] is dual.

Furthermore, although the term *svargakāma* (one who desires heaven) there stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb, it does not have the agent as its primary meaning; rather, it refers exclusively to the object-to-be-accomplished (*bhāvya*) called heaven, which is presented through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And the nominative case-ending (*prathamā*) there, by secondary indication, has the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, even on the strength of that coreferentiality, there is no secondary indication of the locus (*āśraya*) by the verb. However, the cause for the employment of the nominative is everywhere the expression of agency (*kartṛtva*). Whether that [agency] has agency as its qualifier (*prakāra*) or agency as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is another matter. Therefore, it is established that even in the verb, there is secondary indication of agency and so forth.

Regarding the arguments for the primary qualificandhood (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*) of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*): even that [agent] is not the qualificand with respect to the efficient force; rather, the efficient force itself is the qualificand of that [agent]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "pacati brūte" ("he says while cooking"), because that [agent] would be as fit [as a subject] as in the case of "pakttā brūte" ("the cooker says"). Furthermore, there would be the non-occurrence of the usage cited in the Bhāṣya, namely "pacati bhavati" ("he is cooking").

As for the cited usage, "apākṣīdbhavati, pakṣyati-bhavati" (he was cooking, he will cook—[it] is), that is not improper, because it is accepted that the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) consists in the fact that the past and future acts of cooking (*pāka*), which are the locus of the mental disposition (*bhāvanā*), possess a present connection (*yuktatva*) through the root *bhū* used in the sense of "being connected.

Furthermore, the usage "bhavati" is observed in common worldly usage in the sense of "is connected" (*yujyate*). Likewise, the usage "pacati bhavati" (he is cooking) [is valid] under the view that the agent is the primary qualificand (*kartṛviśeṣyatvapakṣe*).

This is not tenable; for if that were the case, it would result in the improper usage of forms such as *pacanti bhavanti* ("they cook, they exist"). Furthermore, according to the Nirukta tradition which states, "a verb is primarily denotative of the process of becoming" (*bhāvapradhānam ākhyātam*), the process of becoming (*bhāvanā*)—which is distinct from the mere meaning of the verbal suffix—is declared to be the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the entire meaning of the verb. For in this context, it is not understood that the process of becoming is primary with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*).

By the very traditional rule (smṛti), "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, but between those two, the suffix [expresses it] primarily," it is established that the predominance of the suffix-meaning as determined by the base-meaning applies universally to the meanings of *sup*-suffixes as well.
This constitutes the refutation of the Vaiyākaraṇa position that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) alone is the "substantive entity" (*bhāvapadārtha*).

Nor should it be argued that the view of the Grammarians alone is correct—on the grounds that, since the word *bhāva* is determined by the grammatical tradition (*vaiyākaraṇasmṛti*) stating "the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*), being purely and simply the action (*bhāva*), is called *bhāva*," this tradition restricts the primacy of that very meaning over the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*), while the tradition regarding the primacy of the suffix-meaning must be explained as referring generally to the meanings of nominal suffixes (*subartha*)—because this [latter] is merely a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*).

Because, like the increase of a river and so forth, it does not apply elsewhere; for this very reason, its application occurs only in the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) in such rules as "the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*)," yet even that does not apply everywhere, since it does not apply in cases such as "the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). Therefore, by the word *bhāva* in the *Nirukta*, through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the root *bhū* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) followed by the suffix *ac*, it is specifically the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)—in the form of an operation conducive to becoming—that is expressed, and not the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). For this very reason, based on the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating "all nouns are born from verbs," and concluding that the word "verb" (*ākhyāta*) refers to the verbal root, it follows from this rule as well that [the *bhāvanā*] belongs to the verbal root alone.

The argument that the predominance of the *bhāva* (the action/state) necessitates that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) be the primary qualificand is refuted; for it has been established in the *Kaustubha* that since the term "verb" (*ākhyāta*) is not applied to words ending in *kṛt*-suffixes such as *pācaka*, the word "verb" in that context is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) with respect to the verbal root. Therefore, when there is a plurality of meanings denoted by a verb, and the question arises as to which is primary and which is subordinate, the traditional rule (*smṛti*)—"A verb has the *bhāva* as its primary [meaning]"—restricts that the *bhāvanā* alone is primary with respect to the other meanings of the verb, excluding the *bhāvanā* itself. For this very reason, [the *bhāvanā*] is one, being common to [all factors] such as time (*kāla*).

The meaning of the suffix *laṭ* is presentness (*vartamānatva*). This consists in having a time non-different from the time of the utterance of the *laṭ*. And this [presentness] connects with the action (*kṛti*) by way of the relation of temporal occurrence (*kālikavṛttitvasambandha*), because at least one action within the collection of actions that bring about the softening (*viklitti*) occurs at the time of that utterance. In all these instances, the word "action" (*kṛti*) refers to productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

Therefore, in expressions such as "he knows" (*jānāti*), there is no defect, because the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is present. In cases such as "it perishes" (*naśyati*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses destruction itself, while the suffix (*pratyaya*) indicates counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). The present time then conjoins with that very counter-positiveness by way of the relation "being the state of having a destruction whose origination resides in itself," in accordance with the constraints of actual experience.

And thus, in our view, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is precisely this: "the counter-positiveness of the destruction residing in the jar [is such] like presentness, by way of the relation of being a destruction produced at the present time. Furthermore, one need not assume that the root indicates "origination" (*utpatti*), and that time somehow connects with that [origination]. Thus, even though there are different relations, the present time connects only with the verbal base (*dhātu*) everywhere; there is no assumption of any other qualificandum for it. As for the removal of the suspicion regarding the infinity of causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) when there is connection through different relations: [The answer is: There is no fault, because the relation between the qualifier and the qualified is fixed by the nature of the thing (*svarūpa-sambandha*). Or, the relation is fixed by the fact that the cognition of the qualifier is the cause of the cognition of the qualified. Or, the relation is fixed by the fact that the cognition of the qualified is the effect of the cognition of the qualifier. Therefore, the suspicion of an infinite regress of causal relations is dispelled. Thus, everything is consistent.

Nor should it be argued that even when a single qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) is obtained, the problem of the infinite number of cause-and-effect relations for the cognition of co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra-jñāna*) due to the difference in relations remains as it was. For, although there is a factual difference in the specific relations, it is possible to establish a single such relation by taking the general property of "relation" (*sambandha-sāmānya*); that is, the cognition of co-occurrence is the cause with respect to the verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*) characterized by having that [general relation] as its qualifier and that [single qualificandum] as its qualificandum. Thus, since the lack of uniformity (*ananugama*) regarding the specific relations is not a defect, [the theory holds].

For just as, despite the differences between relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and temporal relation (*kālika*), when a verbal cognition arises from a sentence such as "the substance possesses a jar" (*ghaṭavaddravyam*)—which has a relation in general as its mode of connection, the jar as its qualifier (*prakāra*), and the substance possessing the jar as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*)—and subsequently, upon a desire to know the specific nature of that relation, the intention (*tātparya*) is determined by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to reside in one particular relation alone, the finality of that verbal cognition is reached precisely in that relation.

Where there is an intention (*tātparya*) toward multiple [objects], there the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) culminates in those multiple [objects]. In that case, since the cognition of a relation—even if it is actually the object of the intention—in its specific form depends on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and since in verbal comprehension the relation is cognized only as a relation (i.e., not in its specific individuality), there is no infinite regress in the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for the cognition of such co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) as "the substance is like a jar. It is only by taking the resulting comprehension (*paryavasitabodha*) into account that the relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) or obstructed and obstructor (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*) with respect to a sublation-cognition (*bādhavuddhi*) is established.

Therefore, even when the cognition "this is not a substance possessing a jar" exists through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the cognition "this is a substance possessing a jar" that arises must terminate by resorting to another relation; for it is established by one's own experience that its apparent objective status as having conjunction as its object is sublated. Alternatively, in cases such as "the jar does not exist," one should consider the distinction between relations consisting of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by conjunction, inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth.

Thus, even though there is a difference in the types of qualifiers (*viśeṣya-prakāra*), there is no resulting infinity [of relations] because the property that subsumes them (*anugamaka-dharma*) is one; for the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) does not differ simply because there is a difference in qualifiers such as white or red, or a difference in the qualified objects (*viśeṣya*) such as a jar or a cloth, regarding the non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the meaning of a noun and its referent. Or, let it be that such a difference exists everywhere in these cases; nevertheless, at the time of postulating a single causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), it is more appropriate to assume that the specific [qualifier] presented therein serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) in another causal relation. Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*).

Since it is established by both parties that words ending in the second case (accusative) and so forth cannot be free from expectancy without a verbal action-word (*kriyāpada*), a word expressing an action must necessarily express the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, within that [action], it is appropriate to assume that the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)—which is the qualificand with respect to both the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and time and other factors—is the primary qualificand. This is because, according to the maxim, "When it is possible for the primary qualificand to be the [principal] qualificand, it is improper for it to be a qualifier," and because this conforms to the parsimony of the presentation of the qualificand. Nor is it the case that...

There is no evidence that a word ending in the nominative case requires a verb; for even the mere word "Caitra" generates a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) because it is itself expectancy-laden (*sākāṅkṣa*).

Nor can it be argued that there is no evidence for its requiring a verb simply because a verbal cognition arises when it is used in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as "learned" (*paṇḍita*);

for according to the traditional rule of Kātyāyana—"the verb *as* (to be), in the third person, though not explicitly uttered, is present"—that nominative form also possesses expectancy for a verbal element.

The term *bhavantīparaḥ* means "ending in the present tense" (*laṭ*). Nor is this grammatical rule (anuśāsana) redundant on the grounds that the supply of another verbal form (*kriyāpada*) is also necessary according to semantic fitness (*yogyatā*).

This is because, even when such fitness is common [to other cases], the rule serves to restrict the supply [of the verb] in instances such as the Vedas where there is an absence of apprehension of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Furthermore, its purposefulness is established by its function of dispelling the misconception that the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) must be that which ends in the nominative case (*prathamānta*). Nor can it be argued that, in this case, there is no evidence for the expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) of the verb in instances other than the first person, such as "I am learned" (*ahaṃ paṇḍitaḥ*) or "you are learned" (*tvaṃ paṇḍitaḥ*).

In that regard as well, with respect to a verbal cognition qualified by having the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as its qualifier (*prakāra*), the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a noun-base (*subanta*), related through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). And with respect to a verbal cognition qualified by having the meaning of a case-ending (*sup*)—excluding gender and number—as its qualifier, the cause is the mental presentation produced by a verb-base (*tiṅanta*).

This is because only those [words] whose causal relationship has been established possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For this very reason, even in the first instance, it is not the *caitra* presented by the nominal stem alone that is construed with the action; rather, it is precisely that which is presented by the nominative case-ending. This is even more so when the view is held that the nominative expresses a factor of action (*kāraka*) already denoted [by a verbal suffix].
Therefore, it is established that, in accordance with parsimony (*lāghava*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) alone is the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) in all cases.
[The following concerns] the doubt and its resolution regarding the status of the efficient force as the primary qualificand.

Nor should it be argued that, in accordance with empirical experience, one may accept a multiplicity of linguistic conventions (*vyutpatti*) such that, through compatibility (*yogyatā*), the direct relation of each [word] connects with its respective qualificandum; for if that were the case, then even in examples such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), since there is an experience of the king connecting directly through the relation of owner and owned, one would have to accept a different convention in the case of compounds. Consequently, the connection of the man with the king itself—through a relation of difference (*bheda*)—would be established, resulting in the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) must possess a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, in cases such as *ardhapippalī* (half-pippalī), there would be the undesirable consequence that figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) could not apply to the subsequent member of the compound. Moreover, in sentences such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), since the status of being a means to heaven is perceived in relation to the sacrifice, one must admit that this is an object of mental cognition; otherwise, the kind of verbal comprehension accepted by you—namely, "the one desiring heaven possesses an effort conducive to a sacrifice that has become a means to a desired end"—would be impossible on the basis of the established linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).

Therefore, since the directly perceived relation can be accounted for either as a constituent of an indirect (paramparā) relation or as an object of mental cognition (*mānasabodha*), there is no justification—supported by valid evidence—for postulating a new linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that would require abandoning the convention already established first. Consequently, it is established that in all cases, the present tense (*vartamānakāla*) is construed only with the action (*kṛti*). In this way, the meaning of the *liṅ* suffix—which consists of remoteness qualified by pastness not belonging to the current day—also connects with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force). Among these, "pastness" (*bhūtatva*) is the state of possessing a moment that is the counter-positive of a destruction co-temporal with the utterance of the *liṅ*. And this [pastness] connects with the action (*kṛti*) through a temporal relation; moreover, this applies only to the final action. Therefore, even in a case such as cooking that is accomplished over several days, the *liṭ* suffix usage "he cooked" (*papāca*) does not occur at the time of the destruction of the initial action. Alternatively, [pastness may be defined as] being the counter-positive of a destruction co-temporal with the utterance of the *liṅ*.

That [the meaning of the optative suffix] also connects with the action performed last by way of the relation of identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*). Alternatively, the meaning of the optative suffix is simply the time of its utterance; or rather, it is the optative suffix itself, as before. And its connection with that [action] occurs through relations such as being the counter-positive of a destruction residing in itself (*svavṛtti-dhvaṃsa-pratiyogitva*). In cases such as "he perished" (*nanāśa*), the connection with pastness (*bhūtatva*) is as before. [Likewise,] non-recentness (*anadyatanatva*)...

The property of occurring on a day different from the day of the utterance of the *liṭ* suffix is [one condition]. The property of being "out of sight" (*parokṣatva*) is the state of not being the object of a cognition possessing such a content as "I directly perceive [this]. Both of these properties apply to the action (*kṛti*). However, the first applies through a direct relation, whereas the second applies through the relation of being delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which is related to itself. This is because, since the action residing in Caitra is not an object of the speaker's direct perception, it would be pointless to convey the absence of that [perception] with respect to it.

Alternatively, let it be understood that there is an absence in that [past action] of the quality of being an object of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), which is well-established in the case of what is produced by oneself. Even in the case of the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*), mediacy (*pārokṣya*) should be seen as resulting from a lack of attention. However, the verbal suffix (*śakti*) has power with respect to each of the three meanings [the agent, the action, and the time], because there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*) for determining a specific qualifier-qualified relationship. Therefore, even in the aforementioned definition, there is no status as a qualifier, due to the absence of a decisive factor. As for the meaning of the *luṅ* suffix (the aorist)—in examples such as *apākṣīt*—it is futurity (*bhāvitva*) qualified by non-recentness (*anadyatanatva*). And this [futurity], consisting in the possession of a moment that is the counter-positive of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) existing at the time of the utterance of the *luṅ*, is connected to the first [element of the] action, as previously described.

The meaning of *lṛṭ* (the periphrastic future) in examples such as *pakṣyati* is likewise the general state of futurity, common to both the non-remote (*anadyatana*) and remote (*anadyatana*) [future], in that very same sense.
*Leṭ* occurs only in the Veda, and its meaning is identical to the meaning of *liṅ*, as in "He sacrifices the *samidh*s" (*samidho yajati*).

The meaning of *loṭ* is also identical to the meaning of *liṅ*, namely injunction (*praiṣa*) and so forth, as well as the meanings of the *kṛtya* suffixes. This is because, in the rule "In the cases of injunction (*praiṣa*), permission (*atisarga*), and the arrival of the time (*prāptakāla*), the *kṛtya* suffixes [are used] and also *loṭ*" (*praiṣātisargaprāptakāleṣu kṛtyāśca*), the word "and" (*ca*) carries over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the *loṭ* from the previous rule.

The meaning of *laṅ* is the state of being past and not belonging to the current day; this is established by the rule "anadyatane laṅ," which follows from the governing term "bhūte" (in the past) in the example *apacad*. The meaning of *liṅ* has already been explained previously.
The meaning of *luṅ* is merely the state of being past, as in *apākṣīt*.
The meaning of *lṛṅ*, however, is the non-occurrence (*kriyātipatti*) of an action qualified by the relation of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*), as in: "If there had been good rain, then..."

"...there would have been plenty of food. Here, because there is a relationship of cause and effect between rain and plenty of food, and because both are unaccomplished, there is the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*). This [suffix] occurs in the sense of the future and the past. For example, one sees the following usage even in the past: "I saw your son wandering for the sake of food, and another twice-born man seeking alms from a Brahmin; had he seen him, then he would have eaten, but he did not eat," and so forth.
In these two meanings, the connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) occurs directly through its own essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

And here, in all instances of the *lakāras*, the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) should be understood as either the specific nature of each respective *lakāra*, or, according to the method to be explained later, the specific nature of each respective substitute (*ādeśa*).

In every case, it is established that the meaning of these [suffixes] is construed only with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). This is the manner of the construction of the meaning of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

Thus, the meaning of the *ātmanepada* suffixes and so forth, which consists of a specific type of "appropriation" (*upagraha*)—namely, the result [of the action] going to the agent—also relates to that very [action], by way of a relation such as being its object (*karmatā*). Even though this [result] is expressed by words such as *svargakāma* ("desiring heaven") in the form of "heaven-ness" (*svargatva*) and so on, its designation by the *ātmanepada* suffixes as "going to the agent" and so forth is not untenable. Alternatively, let it be that the meaning of those suffixes is simply "going to the agent" and so on; and that [meaning] is connected with the effort (*kṛti*), by way of a relation such as being the object of a result whose locus is itself. This is the manner of connection for the number expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

In this same way, even a number such as singularity, when expressed by suffixes like *tiP*, is construed with that very [action] through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and not directly with the agent and so forth; for there is no evidence for restricting the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "the action is the primary element" (*bhāvapradhānam*), and because it would result in the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating causal relations and the like.

In that regard, even in instances where the agent is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), as in "Caitra cooks rice" (*caitreṇaudanaḥ pacyate*), the meaning of the suffix is indeed *kṛti* (volitional effort), according to the analysis: "By means of cooking, Caitra produces rice. Here, the cooking is understood as the object (*karman*) and Caitra as the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, the object is indicated by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), in accordance with the grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*). As for the result, such as the softening of the rice, it is not the meaning of any word, because it is already obtainable from other sources.

For this very reason, the view that the fruit (*phala*) is the meaning of the middle-voice suffix (*ātmanepada*) and that effort (*kṛti*) is the meaning of the instrumental case is also refuted. This is because, in examples such as "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*), the denotation of effort is necessarily required even there; thus, to assume multiple denotative powers (*śakti*) would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, in the sentence "Rice is being prepared by Caitra" (*caitreṇa odanaḥ kriyate*), effort is explained as distinct from the rice itself via the instrumental case. Consequently, since effort alone is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in that context, its connection with singularity is not untenable, provided it is related to the act of cooking—which produces the result in the form of softening (*viklitti*) residing in the rice—by way of the relation of being the instrument of that action. [This concludes] the determination of the meaning of the intransitive verbal suffix (*bhāvākhyāta*).

Similarly, even in the case of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) expressing the *bhāva* (action/state), such as in "sleeping is done by Caitra" (*caitreṇa supyate*) or "staying is done by the sky" (*gaganena sthīyate*), it is the *bhāvanā* alone that is expressed, because the verbal suffix is explained as "sleeping is performed. Even in the case of "is stayed" (*sthīyate*), there is the sense of being the locus (*āśrayatva*). Nor is there a lack of evidence for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in that instance; for just as in "Caitra knows" (*caitro jānāti*) and similar cases, the connection with the meaning of the verbal root which has become a qualifier is the basis for figurative indication, so too in "is stayed by the sky" and similar cases, the connection with the meaning of the verbal root which has become a qualifier is logically established as the basis for figurative indication.

Nor is it the case that in those instances there is a cognition having only the meaning of the verbal root as its qualificand; for elsewhere it has been established that the knowledge of a word functions as a cause with respect to a cognition whose nature is delimited by being a cognition of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) as its qualifier. Thus, just as in cases such as "He sacrifices the *samidhs*" (*samidho yajati*), there is the necessity of supplying a word ending in the nominative case, so too, since it has been established elsewhere that the knowledge of the verbal root-word functions as a cause with respect to a verbal cognition whose nature is delimited by having the meaning of the verbal root as its qualifier, this requirement is fulfilled even in the case of the *bhāva*-suffixes (*bhāvākhyāta*) through the assumption of the relation of "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*). In that case as well, [it is said] "the *bhāva* is the primary..."

Due to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that the meaning of the suffix is primary, and due to the traditional rule that the meaning of the suffix is predominant, the action (*bhāvanā*) itself is indeed primary. Furthermore, by the force of grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), the verbal root (*ākhyāta*) indicates the meaning of the verbal base (*dhātvartha*)—which consists of the action—as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), just as it indicates the agent or the object. Thus, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is: "the state of being the substratum of persistence, which resides in the sky and possesses persistence."

The understanding of the persistence [of the action] on a second occasion is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of establishing its correctness. Therefore, even the singular number in "it persists" (*sthiyate*) conveys only the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*), by way of the relation of being determined by the meaning of the verbal root—which is an action (*bhāva*) that has itself as its substratum. This is because there is no evidence for restricting the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "the action is the primary element" (*bhāvapradhānam*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of dual or plural endings when one intends to express duality or plurality of the meaning of the verbal root; for, by the force of the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*) supported by the absence of such usage, duality and so forth are indicated by the singular ending alone.

For this very reason, based on the statement of the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*, "The camel-sitting (*uṣṭrāsikā*)—they sit," the plural number even in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) is merely occasional. Similarly, according to the rule "That which has an action equal to that of the object by means of the object [is treated like the object]," in cases such as "the rice cooks itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayam eva*), where there is a desire to express agency (*kartṛtva*) rather than a desire to express the "object-ness" (*karmatva*)—which is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) residing in the object-factor (*kāraka*) of a transitive root—the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) takes up that very factor as a subordinate element (*guṇatvena*). This is in accordance with the analysis provided by the verbal suffix.

Since the act (*kṛti*) is understood through its capacity alone, the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) resides in that very act by way of the relation of being the producer of the cooking, which in turn produces the result in the form of softening (*viklitti*) that defines it; and the boiled rice (*odana*) is construed [with the act] by way of the relation of being the prompter of the result that defines its own status as the object (*karmatva*). This is clearly explained in the *Kaustubha*.

Thus it is established that every meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) other than *bhāvanā* functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*) precisely with respect to *bhāvanā*, and therefore *bhāvanā* possesses the status of the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣyatva*). However, its status as a qualificand with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is beyond dispute by virtue of the traditional rule (*smṛti*): "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together; however, between those two, the suffix [expresses] primarily. For this very reason, it does not function as a qualifier with respect to another meaning of the suffix; for when it is possible for it to reside in the qualificand, it is improper for it to reside in a qualifier. Thus ends the *Bhāṭṭatantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Khaṇḍadeva.
The doctrine of Bhāvanā is completed. Now follows the determination of the meaning of verbal roots (dhātvartha), including the presentation of Maṇḍana Miśra’s view and its refutation.

Now, what is this so-called "meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*)? On this point many scholars disagree. Among them, Maṇḍana Miśra maintains that the result itself—such as the softening [of rice] and the like—is the meaning of the verbal root; whereas the entire collection of operations, such as blowing and so forth, which are conducive to that result, constitute the meaning of the suffix by virtue of being "operations" (*vyāpāra*), and the result stands as the qualifier (*prakāratva*) with respect to it.

That is not correct; for it would result in the improper usage "the village is the substratum of the conjunction produced by going," because the fruit called conjunction, being identical with the act of going itself, cannot be produced by it. Furthermore, it would result in the improper usage "the village is the substratum of going. Nor can it be argued that such usages do not arise because the suffix *lyuṭ* denotes the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and thus expresses an operation; for even so, the usage "the village possesses the meaning of 'going'" would still result, and the usage "the village is the substratum of the conjunction produced by the meaning of 'going'" would still not be possible.

If the result, known as the destruction of ownership (*svatva-dhvaṃsa*), were the meaning of the verbal root *yaji* (to sacrifice), then that very result would become the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the efficient force of the result (*phala-bhāvanā*), thereby resulting in its being the means to heaven; furthermore, since the arising of heaven could be accounted for by that [destruction] alone—which is enduring—there would be no need to postulate an *apūrva*.
This is the view of the ancient grammarians (*śābdika*) that the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is merely an operation (*vyāpāra*).

Therefore, others maintain that the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is merely "activity" (*vyāpāra*), while the "result" (*phala*) is the meaning of the accusative case. This too is not correct; for if activity were denoted as such [in general], all verbal roots would become synonyms. And if it were denoted in its specific form as "action-ness" (*kriyātva*) and so forth, then *tyaj* (to abandon) and *gam* (to go) would also become synonyms. The meaning of *tyaj* is an action conducive to separation from a preceding location, while that of *gam* is that same action conducive to conjunction with a succeeding location. Thus, if the verbal root denotes mere activity and the accusative denotes the result in general, then those two [roots] would necessarily become synonyms.

An exposition of the view of the Neo-Grammarians (Navya-Vaiyākaraṇas) regarding the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*): Therefore, both [the action and the result] constitute the meaning of the root, and there is a separate denotative power (*śakti*) for each. Consequently, there is no possibility of the object of the word *odana* (boiled rice) being construed as a part of [only one of] these two. Between the two, the relation is that of the produced and the producer (*janyajanakabhāva*). Furthermore, the resulting cognition has the operation (*vyāpāra*) as its primary qualificand. In that very [operation], all case-factors (*kārakas*) other than the objective factor (*karman*) are construed; the objective factor, however, is construed with the result. The operation is to be expressed as residing in the body—such as blowing (*phūtkāra*) and so forth—or as residing in the self (*ātman*), such as effort (*prayatna*) and so forth.

This is because it is impossible for a single, distinct property that has been followed [as a qualifier] to be produced [as the primary object]. Nor does it follow that all the operations of the various *kārakas* would result in the word having multiple meanings (*nānārthakatva*) on the grounds that they must be denoted as such; for if this consequence were accepted, it would follow that all *kārakas* would have to appear in the nominative case (*prathamāntatā*). Even if there is multiplicity of meaning, when the operation of a particular *kāraka* is intended to be expressed at a given time, only that operation is understood, just as in the case of [the word] "tat" and so forth, where that which resides in the intellect is what is conveyed.

Furthermore, at that time, only that which is the agent (kāraka) possesses the status of being the subject (prathamānta). For this very reason, even such usages as "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*) are consistent when intended in that sense. Therefore, every activity whatsoever is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). However, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is: in cases with verbal suffixes such as *yak* (e.g., *yajati*), it is the object (*karman*); in cases with suffixes such as *śap* (e.g., *pacati*), it is the agent (*kartṛ*); and in cases following intransitive roots (e.g., *bhavati*), it is the meaning of the root itself in the form of a state (*bhāva*). This is according to the grammatical rule: "The *l*-suffixes [denote] the object... and so forth.

And all [factors] possess the status of a subordinate (guṇa) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) through a suitable relationship. This is because the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating "the verb is primarily concerned with the action" (*bhāvapradhānamākhyātam*) establishes that the meaning of the verbal root—denoted by the word *bhāva*—is primary with respect to the meaning of the finite verb (*ākhyātārtha*). Grammarians maintain, however, that the traditional rule regarding the primacy of the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*) refers specifically to the domain of nominal suffixes (*subādi*). [The following is] the refutation of the grammarians' position:

That too is not correct; for blowing and so forth are not understood from the word "pacati" (he cooks), and it is impossible for that which does not appear [in the cognition] to be the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, even in the absence of blowing and so forth, when rice is produced by a flame established by its own nature through another action belonging to Caitra, the usage "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*) occurs.

Furthermore, there would be no room for the disagreement among disputants as to whether the object of experience—be it the specific activity—is a sacrifice (*yāga*), a desire (*icchā*), or a cognition (*jñāna*). Therefore, the "cookability" (*pākatva*) being experienced, or "sacrificeness" (*yāgatva*) and so forth, is precisely a generality residing in the activities that bring about their respective results; this is the delimitor of the denotative power (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of words such as *pac* ("to cook"). When that [generality] exists, the uniform cognition "cooking, cooking," etc., serves as the proof (*pramāṇa*). This is established either by its being the delimitor of the capacity to produce a result, or simply by its being the delimitor of the denotative power.

Its establishment [is as follows]: the understanding of the property of being an operation that brings about a result (*phalopadhāyakavyāpāratva*) and so forth arises from other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), and not from verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

For this very reason, even the result (*phala*) is not understood by means of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), because it will be established that the meaning of that [case] is only "objectness" (*karmatva*) in the form of an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).
And the delimitors of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) are the respective natures of those various verbal roots (*dhātutva*).

The definition of the object *pāka* (cooking) and its universal property *pākatva* (the state of being cooking) reside only in the operation (*vyāpāra*) that produces softening (*viklitti*), and not also in the effort (*yatna*) and so forth [that initiate it]. This is because effort and the like are explained as distinct from the cooking itself in such expressions as “I am doing the cooking” (*pākaṃ karomi*). Nor can it be argued that the separate explanation is justified by the assumption that the verbal root, when co-occurring with suffixes such as *ghañ*, has its denotative power (*śakti*) restricted solely to the result (*phala*); for this would involve the fault of complexity (*gaurava*), whether due to assuming multiple denotative powers or assuming a power that obstructs the power directed toward the operation.

Furthermore, because of the fear of incurring a transgression (āpatti) based on the cognition that "the village has gone," it is also necessary to understand the activity (*vyāpāra*). For this very reason, the meaning of the word *pāka* (cooking) is simply the collection of activities that produce softening (*viklitti*), and not even the effort (*yatna*) that produces it; for since that [effort] is explained separately, it does not constitute the meaning of the root *pac*. For this same reason, the objection that the meaning of *pac* is merely contact with fire (*tejassaṃyoga*), rather than the general activity conducive to softening, is also refuted.

This is because the usage "he cooks" (*pacati*) occurs even in the case of one who possesses no effort conducive to contact with fire, but is instead performing the act of pouring out (*avasrāvaṇa*) which is conducive to the softening of the food.

Therefore, when there arises a desire to know the cause of the manifestation of effort and so forth—which appear as distinct from the act of cooking—it follows by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that these are indeed the meanings of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Furthermore, in that case, the status of "qualifier" (*prakāratva*) belongs to the cooking and so forth precisely because they are the meanings of the verbal root (*prakṛti*). And thus, the traditional rule regarding the predominance of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not contradicted.
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of the verbal root in the *Bhāṭṭatantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Khaṇḍadeva.
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). According to the view of Pārthasārathi Miśra, the explanation of the meaning of the verbal suffix is as follows:

here, the general activity conducive to cooking and so forth is indeed the meaning of the suffix, as expressed by the causative form of the root *bhū* in the phrase "he brings about the cooking" (*pākaṃ bhāvayati*).

This is because the analysis [of the term *pacati*] is provided by means of a word expressing general activity (*vyāpāra*). As for the analysis "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), that too is entirely consistent, since the verb *karoti* expresses general activity. For *karoti* does not have "effort" (*yatna*) as its meaning; if it did, it would follow that *karoti*, like the verb *yatati*, would be intransitive (i.e., take no object).

For a verbal root (*dhātu*) is transitive (*sakarmaka*) when it denotes an operation (*vyāpāra*) that has a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) from its result (*phala*); it is intransitive (*akarmaka*) when it denotes an operation that has the same locus as its result. In the case of *pacati* ("he cooks"), the result is softening (*viklitti*), which resides in the rice (*odana*), while the operation resides in Caitra; thus, because they have different loci, it is transitive. In the case of *svapiti* ("he sleeps"), the result is pleasure (*sukha*), and that resides in Caitra himself; thus, because both [result and operation] share the same locus, it is intransitive.

If, therefore, *karoti* and *yatati* have the same meaning, then it would be contradictory for a single object to be both the locus of the result (*phala*) and not the locus of the result; hence, *karoti* also must denote action (*vyāpāra*) in general.

For this very reason, even the analysis of the sentence "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*) as "the chariot performs going" (*ratho gamanaṃ karoti*) is consistent. Therefore, because it is analyzed by means of the verbs *karoti* (he does) and *bhāvayati* (he brings about), the meaning expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) must be a general activity (*vyāpāra-sāmānya*) distinct from the specific meaning of the root (*prakṛta-dhātvartha*), which has the fruit as its objective. Furthermore, whether that fruit is the meaning of the root itself or something like heaven (*svarga*) is another matter. Regarding the requirement for a specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—which takes the form of a desire for particulars—of that general activity, Pārthasārathi maintains that the provision of those particulars is made by sentences such as those concerning the *prayāja* offerings.
Herein lies the internal dissatisfaction [with the opponent's view] and his own position: that effort (*yatna*) alone is the denotation of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

In reality, however, because there is no single, light, and recurring *śakyatāvacchedaka* (the delimitor of the denotative capacity) that could encompass all instances through the differences in their respective results or the differences in their respective operations—as evidenced by the analyses such as "he cooks" = "he exerts effort toward cooking" or "he performs cooking"—the property of effort (*yatnatva*) itself is the *śakyatāvacchedaka* for the verbal suffix. Nor is the root *kṛ* a denoter of an operation conducive to that effort; for even when Caitra is trembling due to a wind-disease (*vātaroga*), he possesses an operation in the form of a specific conjunction with air that is conducive to that trembling, yet he is not said to be "acting."

"I do not perform the movement; rather, my body moves due to a wind-disease"—from such a cognition, it is understood that the root *kṛ* (to do) has "effort" (*yatna*) as its meaning. Furthermore, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in taking "effort-ness" (*yatnatva*) as the delimitor of the denotation (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Thus, in expressions such as "the chariot performs going," it should be noted that the root *kṛ* is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote a favorable operation (*anukūlavyāpāra*).

Nor does it follow that the root *kṛ* (to do) is synonymous with *bhāvaya* (to cause to be), because there is no difference in their having an agent and an object whose state of being (*bhāva*) is the same. Even in the absence of synonymy, it is possible for *kṛ* to have an agent and an object whose state of being is the same, because its delimitor of capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—namely, effort (*yatna*)—is pervaded by the delimitor of capacity of *bhāvaya*. [This concludes] the definition of transitivity and intransitivity.

Nor does it follow that if *kṛ* has "effort" as its meaning, it would be intransitive like *yat*, because even though both have effort as their single common meaning, the distinction between transitive and intransitive status is established by the difference in the fruits that delimit the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthatāvacchedakaphala*). For in the case of *yat*, the fruit—which is co-locus with the effort—is simply the action residing in Caitra; whereas for *kṛ*, the fruit that delimits the meaning of the root is the [action] called "origination," which is non-co-locus with the effort.

And thus, just as in the case of "cooks" (*pacati*) and "goes" (*gacchati*), even though there is unity in the action consisting of the form of the operation (*vyāpāra*), the distinction is established solely on the basis of the difference in the result (*phala*); so too here, even though there is unity in the action consisting of the form of the operation, the establishment of the status of being transitive (*sakarmaka*) or intransitive (*akarmaka*) is possible solely on the basis of the difference in the result. Furthermore, regarding that result, it is another matter whether it is merely indicated (*upalakṣaṇa*) by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—being known through other means of knowledge—or whether it is actually denoted (*vācya*) by the verbal root itself. [This concludes] the refutation of the stated definition and the formulation of another definition.

In reality, however, because this definition is flawed by defects such as under-extension (*avyāpti*) according to the *Kaustubha*, it is more appropriate to define transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) as "the state of being a verbal root that requires an object, qualified by the absence of non-intentionality" (*avivakṣāvirahaviśiṣṭa-karmākāṅkṣa-dhātutvam*), and intransitivity (*akarmakatva*) as the absence thereof. In this context, "requirement" (*ākāṅkṣā*) consists of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) and is a property of words.

Therefore, even though the referent (artha) is one and the same, just as in cases such as "the jar" (*ghaṭaḥ*) and "objecthood" (*karmatvam*), there is a lack of expectancy (*anākāṅkṣatva*), whereas in cases such as "the jar" (*ghaṭam*), there is expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*); in the very same way, although the root *yat* lacks expectancy for an object and the root *kṛ* possesses expectancy for an object, it remains intransitive during a state of non-intention (*avivakṣā-daśā*), and thus there is no absence of intention [to treat it as transitive]. For this very reason, there is usage in the abstract sense (*bhāve*) such as *odanasya pacyate* ("the cooking of rice"). Furthermore, since roots like *ās* and others—which are intransitive by their own nature—possess expectancy for an object when joined with time-periods such as a month, they become transitive; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of such usage as *caitreṇa āsyate māsaḥ* ("Caitra is seated for a month").

Thus, it should be understood that for the very same verbal root *grath* (to tie), there is transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) because, when considered under the property of denoting an operation residing in Caitra, it requires an object; and there is intransitivity (*akarmakatva*) because, when considered as denoting an operation residing in the flower, it does not require an object.

Therefore, even though the meaning of *karoti* is effort (*yatna*), its transitivity remains unimpaired, and consequently, the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) explained by it also has effort as its meaning. And so, in cases such as "the chariot goes," "he knows," "he desires," or "he exerts effort," where effort is precluded, there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of either a favorable operation or the state of being a locus (*āśrayatva*).

In expressions such as "it should be seen" (*draṣṭavyam*) or "it perishes" (*naśyati*), there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*). Thus it is established that, whether in its primary or secondary sense, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) everywhere consists in *bhāvanā* (the efficient force), which is distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Regarding the determination of the delimitor of its denotative power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*): the delimitor of the denotative power of that [suffix] is the nature of being explained by the verb "to do" (*karoti*). Consequently, since there is an absence of explanation by "to do" in cases such as "it exists" (*bhavati*), there is no *bhāvanā*; therefore, according to the ancients, the case-factors (*kāraka*) are construed with the meaning of the verbal root itself, and their connection with singularity and so forth occurs through a mediated relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*).

In reality, however, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the property of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) alone is the delimitor of the denotative power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). In expressions such as *bhavati* ("it exists"), there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the locus (*āśrayatva*). And thus, through the connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth—

Nor can one assume a further linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). Furthermore, the property of being *l* (*latva*) cannot be the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), because it would follow that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) could be understood even from a *lakāra* that is presented in some arbitrary manner. Nor can the *latva* presented by its substitute (*ādeśa*) be the delimitor, because it would follow that the productive operation could be cognized through the denotative capacity even from a *lakāra* presented by substitutes such as *śānac*. Nor can the *latva* presented by substitutes such as *tip* be the delimitor; for if that were the case, since there are many such substitutes as *tip* and others, the delimiters of the denotative capacity would not be uniform, resulting in the undesirable consequence of multiple distinct capacities.

Therefore, the expressive power (śakti) resides in each individual suffix such as *tip* and so forth. For this very reason, verbal cognition occurs even when the *lakāra* (the general verbal suffix) is not presented by means of *tip* and the others. Otherwise, there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating the causality of so many erroneous cognitions of expressive power directed toward the numerous *tip* suffixes and the like.

By this, the following view is refuted: that "the property of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) alone is the delimitor of denotative power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*); and that [property] consists in possessing the status of a verbal suffix by virtue of the relation of being denotable; and since that [status] exists in *ti*, *p*, etc., they are the possessors of denotative power. For even when one does not know that *ti*, *p*, etc., are denotable by the word "verbal suffix," and even when one knows them merely as *ti*, *p*, etc., in instances such as *pacati*, there is still a cognition of productive activity (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, it is established that productive activity is the meaning of the verbal suffix. This concludes the demonstration of the primacy of productive activity.

And in that case, the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is construed as a qualifier (prakāra), because there is no reason to restrict the traditional rule regarding the predominance of the meaning of the suffix (pratyayārtha-prādhānya-smṛti). As for the statement "the action (bhāva) is predominant," when it is asked which among the many meanings of the verb (ākhyāta) is predominant, it is established that the predominance belongs to the productive urge (bhāvanā) expressed by the word "bhāva"; thus, since this successfully provides the required meaning, it is improper to restrict the traditional rule on the predominance of the suffix-meaning. Therefore, it is already stated that in the aforementioned traditional rule, the word "bhāva" does not denote the meaning of the verbal root as defined by grammarians (vaiyākaraṇa-paribhāṣita).

Furthermore, since there is a traditional rule (smṛti) regarding the predominance of the meaning of the suffix, and because it is necessary to restrict the gender, number, and so forth of the meanings of *su*-suffixes and others—which function as qualifiers (*prakara*)—with respect to the meaning of the stem (*prakṛtyartha*), there is no obstacle even in the case of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), provided that in cases such as instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), its predominance with respect to the meaning of the stem has been established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); in such cases, [the rule] serves merely as a restatement (*anuvāda*).

"They both express the meaning of the suffix together, yet between the two, the suffix is primary"—from hearing this [rule], because there is a rule of necessity regarding primacy toward the meaning of the base (prakṛti) by virtue of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of the suffix, there is no harm even though gender, number, and so forth, which are the meanings of the case-endings (*sub*), etc., are not primary.

In reality, however, it will be explained that gender, number, and other such meanings of the suffix are not qualifiers (*prakāra*) of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), but rather, by virtue of the scriptural statement of co-referentiality (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*), they are qualifiers only with respect to other meanings of the suffix, such as the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*). Therefore, it is established that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is a qualifier of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

Thus ends the determination of the meaning of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) in the *Bhaṭṭatantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Khaṇḍadeva. Now begins the determination of the meaning of the verbal root as a qualifier of the productive operation.

In some cases, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself is the qualifier (*prakāra*) of the denoted sense (*śakyārtha*), as in "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*). In other cases, it is the indicated sense (*lakṣyārtha*) alone, as in "one should immolate the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma" (*agnīṣomīyaṃ paśumālabheta*), where the sacrifice (*yāga*) is the indicated sense. Furthermore, even the indicated sense may sometimes be qualified by its own denoted sense, as in "one should stand near with the *pṛṣṭha* hymns," where, in accordance with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the act of expressing [the hymns] is qualified by the denoted sense of standing nearby. However, in reality, in instances such as "one should sacrifice with Soma" and in various injunctions, the indication occurs precisely through the generic nature of a distinct type of sacrifice (*vijātīyayāgatva*); therefore, the connection with the denoted sense must be understood here.
Regarding the connection of the root-meaning with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), there is an investigation into its relation;

and that relation to the effort (*kṛti*) is not "conduciveness," because by the force of the paraphrase "he cooks = he performs cooking," it is understood as a relation consisting precisely in being the object (*karmatva*) of the cooking. For this very reason, in cases such as "he cooks rice," since the paraphrase is "he produces rice by means of cooking," being the instrument (*karaṇatva*) of the cooking is also understood, and thus that too is a relation. Consequently, in all instances, the root-meaning is connected to the productive operation solely through one of these two relations: either as an object or as an instrument. Although cooking is indeed the instrument with respect to the effort, [the relation is still one of these two].

[It may be argued that the relation is] sublated, because cooking and the like are achievable through effort (*kṛti*). Nevertheless, since cooking is construed with effort by way of the relation of "having rice as its objective" which is qualified by "being the instrument residing in itself," the relation is established because instrumentality is also included within the relational complex (*saṃsarga*). Furthermore, rice also possesses a "subjectivity" (*viṣayatā*) called "objectivity" (*uddeśyatā*) toward effort; thus, there is no sublation of such a relation.

Furthermore, in cases where no specific injunction (*vidhi*) is heard, and where a word ending in the accusative case is not heard—as in "Caitra cooks" (*pacati caitraḥ*)—the verbal root-meaning possesses the status of an object (*karman*) even when its being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is unknown. This is because the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) conveyed by the verb suffix is necessarily transitive (*sakarmaka*), just like the meaning of the root *√kṛ* ("to do"). For this very reason, even in the case of intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the productive activity conveyed by the verb suffix is indeed transitive.

For this very reason, when there is an expectancy for that [object] in such cases as "one desiring health should lie down," only health and the like—denoted by the word *kāma* (desire)—are construed as the object (*karman*), just as heaven and the like are [construed] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by the word *svargakāma*. The verbal root (*dhātu*), however, is indeed intransitive (*akarmaka*). For this very reason, the accusative case does not occur here with respect to the object of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*); rather, it occurs only with respect to the object of the meaning of the verbal root itself.

In cases involving transitive roots (*sakarmakadhātu*), such as "he threshes rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) and the like, although those [objects] are first construed as the object (*karman*) of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), they subsequently also function as the object of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*). Thus, the status of those roots as transitive is established. Therefore, because the productive operation is invariably transitive, in instances such as "Caitra cooks" (*pacati caitraḥ*), when the productive operation requires an object, the root-meaning itself serves as that object by virtue of its co-occurrence within the same word (*samānapadaśruti*).

Furthermore, since it is a worldly statement, there is no fault even if it is purposeless. In the Veda, however, because it cannot function as a mere eulogy (ārthavāda) due to its syntactic unity with other injunctions (*vidhi*), and because one must conform to the purposefulness established by the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*), one must either assume that the *laṭ* (present tense suffix) has the sense of the *leṭ* (subjunctive), or assume through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that it conveys the meaning of the *leṭ*. Consequently, having postulated another object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) such as heaven for the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) therein. This is because the injunctive force (*pravartakatva*) of the injunction would otherwise be inexplicable, necessitating that the productive urge expressed in syntactic proximity to it must necessarily have a desirable result as its object to be accomplished.

Because in expressions such as "bring the pot and the cloth," we observe the connection of two objects even without the word *ca* (and), and because—just like the root *kṛ*—the *bhāvanā* expressed by the verbal suffix is restricted to having only one object, it would follow that sacrifices (*yāga*) and the like could not function as its objects. Therefore, wherever another thing to be brought about (*bhāvya*) is indicated by the accusative case or similar means—whether there is co-utterance with an injunction or not—as in "one should thresh rice" (*vrīhīnavahanyāt*) or "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), the meaning of the verbal root functions solely as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

However, in cases where there is no other means of accomplishment (*karaṇa*) available and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not established by context or other factors—such as in the injunctions "One desiring cattle should fetch water in a *godohana* vessel" and "One desiring sensory power should sacrifice with curds"—the verbal root serves merely to restate (*anuvāda*) the meaning of the root already established by context as the substratum (*āśraya*), for the sake of ensuring grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Yet, that meaning is neither construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) nor as the substratum.

Since it is impossible to establish a substratum (*āśrayatva*) that is distinct from the status of being an object (*karmatva*), and since the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is already occupied by the object in the form of the sense-organ (*indriya*), if the *homa* were also construed as an object, there would result the collapse of the unity of the action. For this very reason, in the *Kaustubha* and other works, it is stated that even when there is a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) caused by multiple intended objects, the root cause of the defect is precisely the collapse of the unity of the action. This concludes the investigation into the nature of the unity of the action within the productive activity.

Furthermore, "having a single object" (*ekakarmakatva*) does not mean having one and the same object, nor does it mean having multiple objects that share a single substratum; for this would fail to apply in cases such as "the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [are performed] for all [desires]" or "bring the jar. In those instances, there is a plurality of objects residing in the son and so forth, or a plurality of sons and so forth who are the substrata of those objects. Nor does it mean "having a single object as its delimitor" (*ekakarmatvāvacchedakatva*); for this would fail to apply in cases such as "the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [are performed] for all [desires]" or "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*).

In that regard, although there is a difference between the qualifiers of the objecthood (*karmatāvacchedaka*)—such as "son-ness" and "animal-ness"—and their respective *apūrva*-producing capacities, it is stated in the *Kaustubha* that [the action] possesses the property of being the locus of the pervasion (*paryāpti*) of objecthood, which is the scope of a single cognition. And in all such instances, because a single word generates a single cognition consisting of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) regarding the properties that serve as the loci of the pervasion of objecthood, the status of having a single object is established.

In the case of the statement, "The *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer restrain their speech," there would follow the consequence of it being a transitive verb with two objects (*dvikarmaka*), because the properties of being the *adhvaryu* and being the sacrificer—which serve as the delimiters of the objecthood and the locus-hood [respectively]—would not both be the objects of a single cognition. Therefore, [the relation] is defined as *paryāpti* (pervasion).

In this regard, because it is determined—just as in the case of deityhood (*devatātva*) and so forth—that even objecthood (*karmatva*) and other such properties reside distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) across the members following a *dvandva* compound, the property that delimits the locus of its pervasion (*paryāpti*), namely "the state of being both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer" (*adhvaryuyajamānobhayatva*), is the object of the single cognition produced by the *dvandva*; thus, a single objecthood is logically established. This has been demonstrated in the *Kaustubha* and other works.

Thus, in cases such as "Bring the white pot," the unity of the object of action (*karmatva*) is established either through non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) of "white" with the "pot" by means of both words, or through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a pot qualified by the quality of whiteness by the word "pot" alone. Similarly, in cases such as "Bring the pot and the cloth," that [unity] is established through indication in both words ending in the accusative case, in accordance with the intention conveyed by the particle *ca*, which signifies mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).

And just as this being the case, the reason for the defectiveness of sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*)— caused by the multiplicity of things to be enjoined (*uddeśya*) in a situation involving two *nimittas*— is the resulting loss of the status of having a single action (*ekakarmakatva*), as is clear from the *Kaustubha*,

so too it is established that where another object (*bhāvya*) fit for connection with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is presented by a second-case ending (*dvitīyā*) or the like, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) does not possess the status of being the object (*karman*).
[The following are] instances where the meaning of the verbal root connects as the object:

However, where that [instrumentality] is not mentioned, and the fact that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is established by another means of knowledge as being a means to achieve a desired end, then—provided there exists another quality (*guṇa*) to be enjoined by its own sentence—the meaning of the verbal root functions solely as the object (*karman*). This is as in "He offers oblation with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), and so forth. Nor does it follow that in such cases as "He offers oblation with a ladle" (*juhvā juhoti*), the verb *juhoti* would become transitive; for since another object is necessarily required, this would result in the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) having two objects. This is because even for a transitive verb, the non-intentional expression of the object (*karmāvivakṣā*) is possible, just as in the case of the impersonal verb form (*bhāvākhyāta*). Even in such instances, [the same principle applies].
