If, in the context of the ritual application (*viṣaya*), there is the hearing of a name ending in the instrumental case, then it possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) alone; for example, in such passages as "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices on level ground," or "Loudly with the *pravargya*. However, where there is no hearing of such a quality (*guṇa*), there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the verbal root's meaning itself as the object (*karman*) for the sake of another purpose, as in the two *vidvat*-sentences. But in its absence, as in "He sacrifices to Tanūnapāt," it is indeed a distinct action (*karmāntara*) that serves as the instrument; this and other points are clearly explained in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*).

However, in cases where the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is known through valid cognition, and where there is no hearing of a name ending in the instrumental case—as in *udbhidā* and so forth—such as in "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*) or "one should offer the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*), even though no specific desired object is understood from its own sentence, the fact that the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) has a desired end as its objective (*bhāvya*) is understood by the force of the injunction. Thus, accepting that a general desired end is the objective in those cases, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is indeed the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Regarding the term *agnihotram* here, the traditionalists maintain that even the accusative case ending has the sense of the instrumental (instrumentality). In such cases, by virtue of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) within the same word, the object required by the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is the meaning of the verbal root itself; [the suffixes merely express] the number and gender of that very object.

Nor is there an impossibility of [the act] being an object (*karman*) for that which is not known as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), because its connection [to the injunction] is possible by way of being an unintended object (*anīpsitakarman*). Nor is there a contradiction with the instigating nature of the injunction (*vidhi*), because although the cognition that the injunction conveys a desired result to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) is a cause for activity, it is not a cause for the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*); for even in the absence of that [cognition of the result], the verbal cognition of an efficient force (*bhāvanā*) having the oblation (*homa*) as its object is established.

Nor does it follow that there would be no cognition of its being a means to heaven even in the sentence stating the fruit, because that [action] which is connected as something to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) has no further requirement for another thing to be accomplished; for just as there is a cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) for that which is connected as a means by virtue of the injunction itself, so too, even for that which is already understood as achievable through effort, its status as a means to a specific desired object is established either by another sentence in accordance with the requirement of the injunction, or by the *Viśvajit* maxim.

Therefore, those who delight in logic consider it also reasonable that the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is construed as the object (*karma*) alone within the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), as stated by the Prabhākaras. In every respect, it is established that the meaning of the verbal root possesses the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) in relation to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) through a connection characterized either as the object or the instrument (*karaṇa*).
It is the traditional view (*saṃpradāyamata*) that instrumentality, objecthood, and so forth, are indicated (*lakṣya*) by the verbal root.

The traditionalists, however, maintain that by the verbal root (*dhātu*), either objecthood (*karmatva*) or instrumentality (*karaṇatva*)—which functions in its own primary sense—is indicated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Its connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) occurs through one of two relations: being the qualifier of itself, or having as its objective that which qualifies itself; however, objecthood and the like do not themselves function as the relation. If they did, it would result in the futility of the grammatical rule concerning concomitance, which states: "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together."

For it is not logical that those [grammarians] who are engaged in the instruction of word-meanings (*padārtha*) should also be instructors of syntactic relation (*anvaya*). Therefore, even other factors such as "object-ness" (*karmatva*) and "instrumentality" (*karaṇatva*) appear as word-meanings precisely by virtue of their function (*vṛtti*). For this very reason, the instrumental suffix in *jyotiṣṭomena* is also logically accounted for as restating an instrumentality that appears as a word-meaning. This is because it is a general rule that the qualifier and the qualified possess the property of having a form appearing as a mode (*prakāra*). Thus they say.

Thus it is established that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is always a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). It will be explained later that this [productive operation], whether expressed by a finite verb suffix (*ākhyāta*) or by a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*), etc., does not admit connection with gender; therefore, there is no connection with the productive operation when it is expressed by the word *vastu*. Thus ends the determination of the status of the meaning of the verbal root as a qualifier of the productive operation in the *Bhāṭṭatantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Khaṇḍadeva. [Now begins] the determination of the connection of the meaning of case-suffixes (*sub-artha*) with the productive operation, and the meaning of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*).

In this way, it should be understood that even the meaning of the suffix *su* (the nominative case), though distinct from gender and number, is construed with that very [meaning of the base] as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*). For instance, the meaning of the first case (*prathamā*), being distinct from gender and number, is construed as a qualifier within that [meaning]. Nor is there a lack of evidence for its existence in that sense merely because it is uttered for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*); for in the case of address (*sambodhana*), the state of being oriented toward [the speaker] (*abhimukhatva*) also appears, so that [the claim of its absence] is unproven.

And that [denotable object] consists in being a locus of the verbal cognition intended by the speaker—where such a cognition has as its qualifier the state of being the locus of the verbal understanding under discussion, and as its substantive a person other than the speaker; or alternatively, it consists in possessing a state of being the object of the speaker’s intention residing in someone other than the speaker, which is itself determined by a state of objectivity residing in the verbal understanding under discussion. And that very same thing is the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *yuṣmad*. This exists in cases such as "O Devadatta, bring the cow," and also in cases such as "Caitra is bringing the cow for Devadatta," because [Devadatta] possesses the aforementioned type of cognition, or because he possesses the aforementioned state of objectivity.

Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of the daughter-in-law (*snuṣā*) in a context where the use of an addressive sentence directed at a maiden is intended to inform the daughter-in-law; for although the daughter-in-law is indeed the person being addressed (*saṃbodhya*), the act of addressing her is not the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the utterance, and thus the vocative case does not apply to her. However, when the status of being the intended purport is present, the vocative certainly applies. For this very reason, addressing is primary (*mukhya*) only with respect to sentient beings (*cetana*); in the case of insentient things (*acetana*), it is a figurative usage (*gauṇa*) based on the superimposition (*āropa*) of consciousness.
This concludes the determination of the connection of the meaning of the vocative with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

Therefore, in the first example cited, both "facingness" (abhimukhatva) and "agency" (kartṛtva) constitute the meaning of the nominative case. In that context, "inherence" (ādheyatva) is the relation between the nominal stem-meaning and the other [meaning]; and these two [meanings] are connected to the productive operation (bhāvanā) by way of being the object (viṣayatva) and the determiner (nirūpakatva), respectively. In the latter case [the second example], only "facingness" is connected [to the bhāvanā] through the relation of being the object. Even in cases such as "What kind of person is Maitra to Caitra?", there is no impediment to verbal comprehension, because the insertion of a verb—such as "is" (asti) from the rule *astir bhavantīparaḥ*—is necessarily required.

In sentences such as "Let Caitra go to the village" (*caitra maitro grāmaṃ gacchatu*), however, the status of being the person addressed (*saṃbodhyatva*) is construed with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—which is the object of the request expressed by the imperative suffix (*loḍartha*)—via the aforementioned relation, and the state of being prompted by an operation residing in oneself (*svaniṣṭhavyāpāraprayojyatva*) is construed with it via the relation of identity (*svarūpasambandha*). This is because, according to our linguistic intuition, it is precisely the imperative suffix and so forth, which convey those respective meanings, that function as the indicators of the speaker's intention (*tātparyagrāhaka*). And in this regard:

The capacity to denote [the agent] resides specifically in the nominative case endings (*prathamā*) when used in address (*sambodhana*), due to the force of a separate grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*). Words such as *he* serve merely to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). However, in cases such as "being prompted by an action" (*vyāpāra-prayojyatva*), there is only figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, even in the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), in sentences like "Caitra, Maitra goes to the village," that which ends in the nominative does not possess the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), because it serves as a qualifier for another element which is the meaning of the nominative itself; moreover, in that case, there is no connection with the number conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

Therefore, it must be stated that only the cognitive presentation (*upasthiti*) generated by a nominative case-ending word distinct from the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) is the cause for the connection with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). Nor can that [position] be maintained, because it would fail to apply in cases such as "Caitra, bring the cow" (*caitra gām ānaya*), where no such [vocative] is present. Nor can there be an elliptical supply (*adhyāhāra*) of the word *tvam* (you) there; for if that were so, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of using such a construction as "O Brāhmaṇas, you cook" (*brāhmaṇāḥ tvaṃ pacasi*). Furthermore, there is no rule that the referent of the second person pronoun (*yuṣmad-artha*) and the vocative expressing the agent must share the same number, as that would require the postulation of a separate grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*).

By this, the view that [properties] such as being directed toward [an object] (*abhimukhatva*) are always qualifiers (*prakāra*) of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is refuted; for otherwise, in sentences such as "Caitra, Maitra cooks," there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) and so forth being construed with Caitra.

In reality, even in our own view, since it is impossible to prevent the connection of *bhāvanā* with Caitra as the agent in sentences such as "Caitra cooks," the meaning of the nominative case in the vocative is everywhere the vocative itself, and not agency as well. It should be noted that in cases of the second person, such as "Caitra, cook," the verb expresses the agency of that very individual who is being addressed through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, there is no contingency of agency falling upon anyone other than the person being addressed.

Therefore, by virtue of its commonality with the second case and others, it is appropriate in all instances that even the meaning of the first case (*prathamā*) functions solely as a qualifier (*prakāratva*).

Thus ends the determination of the connection of the meaning of the *su*-affixes and the meaning of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) in the *Bhāṭṭatantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Khaṇḍadeva.
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the nominative case (*prathamā-vibhakti*) according to the system of Pāṇini.

The demonstration that the nominative case (*prathamā*) possesses meaning through its connection with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*): It should not be argued that even though the nominative has a meaningful referent in the form of address (*sambodhana*), just as it does for gender and number, there is no meaning distinct from that [stem-meaning]; and since in examples such as *caitraḥ pacati*, there is no object to be qualified (*viśeṣya*) distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem, how can the meaning of the nominative everywhere function as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in common with the accusative and other cases? For it is understood, by the force of grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*), that even the nominative when not used in address possesses a meaning distinct from gender and number. To illustrate, this is the view of Pāṇini: [The sūtra: *prātipadikārthaliṅgaparimāṇavacanamātre prathamā* (Pā. 2.3.46). This prescribes the nominative suffix when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem, gender, measure, or number. Since the word *mātra* ("merely") is used here, it follows that the nominative expresses a meaning distinct from these. Otherwise, the mention of *liṅga* and *parimāṇa* would be redundant, as they are already included within the meaning of the nominal stem. Therefore, the nominative indeed possesses a distinct meaning. Furthermore, the fact that the nominative is taught alongside the accusative and others in the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pā. 2.3.2) indicates that it is intended to express a meaning distinct from those [other cases]. Thus, the nominative is established as having a distinct meaning.

First of all, according to the rule *prātipadikārthaliṅgaparimāṇavacanamātre prathamā* ("the first [case-ending] occurs when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem, gender, measure, and number"), it is simply the meaning of the nominal stem itself. For this is an injunction regarding the denotative capacity (*śakyatva*) with respect to the portion consisting of gender and so forth, just as it is an injunction regarding the denotative capacity with respect to the portion consisting of the meaning of the nominal stem; it does not intend to mean that the first case-ending is grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) only when the meaning of the nominal stem is intended to be expressed by the nominal stem itself, because that would result in redundancy (*vaiyarthyāpatti*) and because it would result in a lack of uniformity (*vairūpyāpatti*). Therefore, the meaning of the first case-ending is simply the referent of the nominal stem, such as Caitra and the like.

Nor should it be argued that even in this case, since the cognition [of the meaning] is established by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone, the nominative case serves merely as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) regarding that portion, and thus the meaning of the nominative does not function as a qualifier (*prakāra*) elsewhere; for we accept that the nominal stem itself indicates the intention (*tātparya*) regarding the specific meaning of the nominative, and thus the meaning of the nominative [functions as a qualifier] elsewhere.

Because there is no obstacle to [the suffix] being a qualifier (*prakāratva*). Otherwise, if one were to include "being distinct from the nominative" (*prathamātiriktatva*) in the causal relation—namely, that the cause for a verbal cognition delimited by having the meaning of a case-ending as its qualifier is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by a word such as a verbal root—there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, there would be the fault of complexity (gaurava) if one were to include the condition of "being distinct from a nominal stem ending in the nominative case" when the meaning of the base functions as a qualifier (prakāra) with respect to the meaning of the suffix. Moreover, it would entail the necessity of postulating a different rule of linguistic usage (vyutpatti) if the bhāvanā and other meanings of the verb were to function as qualifiers with respect to the meaning of the nominative-terminating base. Therefore, for the sake of parsimony (lāghava), the meaning of the nominative—such as Caitra—is also a qualifier within the verbal sense of *bhāvanā* itself, since it is the meaning of the *su*-suffixes.
For this very reason, in such cases, the base-meaning, such as Caitra, does not undergo syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the nominative meaning, Caitra.

Because the distinction-based relation between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is blocked for one who is proficient [in grammar], and because a non-distinction-based relation is not conventionally established [for such a person], the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in that context merely serves to indicate the intended meaning as being qualified by the sense of the nominative case. However, that very [meaning] presented first is what relates to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), which is the meaning of the verb.
In cases such as "The pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), understanding occurs only through the ellipsis of a verbal action.

Nor does its non-connection [with the sentence] follow from the absence of a finite verb (*ākhyāta-pada*) in such cases; for just as in examples like "kāṣṭhaiḥ odanam" (rice with wood), the supply of a verbal action is required, so too in cases like "nīlaḥ ghaṭaḥ" (a blue pot), the supply of the verb "asti" (is) is all the more justified by the rules of grammar. Furthermore, according to the method to be explained later, the word "nīla" [denotes] either the quality of blueness or the universal "blueness" (*nīlatva-jāti*).

Because the suffix following *śata*—whether by indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or secondary indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*)—serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of a substance qualified by the quality delimited by blueness (*nīlatvāvacchinna-guṇa-viśiṣṭa-dravya*), that substance denoted by the suffix following the word [ending in] *śata* does not also undergo syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with "pot" (*ghaṭa*) through the relation of identity (*abheda*). Rather, it connects only with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) conveyed by the verb (*ākhyāta*), as in "it exists like a pot," since the verbal cognition is established through a single rule of linguistic derivation (*ekavyutpatti*). Otherwise, one would have to assume that the meaning of the noun expressing the qualifier connects with another nominal meaning through the relation of identity, and [subsequently]... [the suffix following...]

Furthermore, it would entail the following complexities: first, one would have to assume that even case-endings from the second case (*dvitīyā*) onwards possess the function of denoting the meaning of the base; second, one would have to assume that the rule of grammatical expectancy (*vyutpatti*) regarding the syntactic connection of the base-meaning with the affix-meaning applies only to cases where the base is not a word expressing a qualifier; thus, such a burden of complexity (*gaurava*) would arise. Nor should it be argued that this acceptance of complexity is not a fault because it conforms to the experience of non-difference (*abheda*) between the quality "blue" and the pot, for once the verbal cognition has occurred—where the two nominative meanings and the pot qualified by the blue quality appear as the objects of the agenthood relation within a cognition whose primary qualificand is the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvanā*)—the [subsequent] cognition of that pot...

When there is a dependence on the quality that serves as the delimiter (*paricchedaka*), and when there is a dependence on the genus (*jāti*) for that which is qualified by the quality, the experience of non-difference (*abhedānubhava*) is mental; thus, the experience is established by taking into account the subsequent cognition (*pāścātyabodha*).
As for the manner in which the non-difference between the "red" (*aruṇā*) and the "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*) appears:

it is not the case that because the non-difference appearing through verbal testimony lacks the status of being an object of knowledge arising from the Veda, there would be no fault even if one were to fail to connect the redness with the one-year-old cow in the phrase "by means of the red one-year-old cow. This is because the mental [cognition] which has as its object the matter required by the Veda [is indeed valid].

Because the object of the Veda's purport (*tātparya*) is that which is the object of knowledge [arising from it]. Indeed, neither being the object of the word-function (*pada-vṛtti*) of the Veda, nor being the object of the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by the Veda, is the determinant for being the object of the Veda's purport. For if that were the case, in the instance—"One takes up the horse's halter with the mantra 'They have grasped this rein of immortality'"—the verbal cognition would only take as its object the mere relationship between the mantra and the horse's halter. And since that [relationship] is established by the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*), this sentence would result in being purposeless.

To avoid that [undesirable consequence], since the absence of scriptural indication (laiṅgika-śruti) for what is being inferred would also not fall within the purport of the Veda, it would follow that [the injunction] could not have exclusion (parisaṃkhyā) as its result.

Therefore, the criterion for being the object of the Veda’s purport is simply being the object of a cognition that removes the expectation for the Veda. And this [criterion] remains intact even when there is non-difference between the substance qualified by the quality and the one-year-old cow (ekahāyanī).

This is also necessary for others [who hold different views], because the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is simply the state of being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasāmānyasādhanatva*). Since the referent of words such as "heaven" (*svarga*) functions as a qualifier of the desire, it is impossible for it to enter into a relation of identity with the "desired" object; therefore, the verbal cognition must necessarily be: "The one who desires heaven possesses an effort conducive to a sacrifice that is a means to what is desired. Subsequently, the understanding of the identity between the desired object and heaven is purely mental, and this is the intended meaning of the scripture.

Furthermore, it must be admitted by you as well that it is precisely this cognition, which constitutes the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*), that is obstructed by the ascertainment of a difference between [the means] and heaven, and not the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) itself; thus, there is no room for that objection against me alone.
This concludes the demonstration that the non-difference between the *aruṇā* (red) and the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) is indeed verbal.

If, however, you maintain—out of fear of such a defect—that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is simply the status of being a means to heaven and so forth, whether by primary denotation (*śakti*) or by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and that the words "heaven" and so on merely serve to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*), then I too shall maintain that the meaning of the nominative case following the word "blue" (the substance qualified by the quality) is construed with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) through the relation of agency residing in a pot identical to itself; and the word "pot" serves to indicate the intended meaning even regarding that relation.

It can be said that the meaning of the nominative case following the word "ghaṭa" (pot) [is related] by way of its own occurrence as the agent; and since non-difference (*abheda*) is thus established as being expressed by words (*śābda*), there is no fault whatsoever.

Some, however, say that just as in the case of an injunction regarding a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) one postulates a collection of words expressing the injunctions regarding the qualifiers, here too one must simply postulate another sentence that conveys non-difference. In any case, it is established that the meaning of the nominative case functions as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) through a relation of difference, a status common to the accusative and other cases.

By this, the view of the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas)—that there is a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the referent of a noun such as Caitra (or the referent of the nominative case itself) and the agent expressed by the verb—is also refuted, because there is no evidence for postulating a separate rule of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). Furthermore, there is another argument [against] the relation of non-difference between the agent expressed by the verb and the nominative referent such as Caitra, along with its refutation.

As for the argument that— since in cases such as "he cooks a little" (*stokaṃ pacati*), for the sake of the non-difference relation (*abheda-anvaya*) of the nominal object "a little" with the act of cooking, it is necessary to postulate a causal relation wherein the cause is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a word co-occurring with the aforementioned nominal, and the effect is the verbal cognition characterized by having as its qualifier the meaning of a nominal co-occurring with a meaningless *sup*-suffix (the accusative) through the relation of identity— it is precisely by this [causal relation] that the non-difference relation of Caitra and so on with the agenthood and other roles is established through semantic fitness (*yogyatā*).

That is not so; for the first case-ending (*prathamā*) following the word *caitra* would be meaningless, which contradicts Pāṇini and others, and also contradicts one's own writing. Furthermore, in the case of *stokam*, the meaning of the nominal stem *stoka-* is "smallness" (*stokatva*), while the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), "substratum-ness. Since this [substratum-ness] connects either directly or indirectly with the cooking (*pāka*) and so forth, or with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), the case-ending is not meaningless; thus, the postulation of such a grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) is unestablished.

Even for one who holds that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified by smallness (*stokatva*), in his view as well, non-difference (*abheda*) is the meaning of the accusative case by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And that [non-difference] consists in a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) having smallness as its counter-correlate; it is simply smallness itself. Furthermore, its connection with the act of cooking and so forth occurs precisely through the relation of difference (*bheda*). The resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is thus: "The cooking and so forth possess smallness, which resides in that which is delimited by the possession of smallness," just as [one might say]: "The cloth possesses substanceness, which resides in that which is delimited by substanceness.
Now follows the determination of the meaning of the nominative case (*prathamā-vibhakti*) according to the view of Kātyāyana.

Kātyāyana, however, maintains that the nominative case does not denote the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); for if that were the case, it would follow that the nominal stem lacks the capacity to generate verbal cognition, since its function would be reduced merely to indicating the speaker's intention (*tātparya*). Rather, the meaning of the nominative is simply the state of being a factor (*kāraka*) already expressed by another word.

And in that first case-meaning, which consists of agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, the referent of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), such as Caitra, connects by way of the relation of difference (*bheda*) alone; and number and so forth connect in the same manner as they do with a word ending in an accusative suffix. Thus, there is no need to postulate a separate rule of grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) anywhere. Furthermore, since agency and so forth are indeed the meaning of the verbal root (*kriyāpada*), just like the meaning of other *su*-suffixes, there is no such [need] even there. Nor is the understanding redundant, because agency and so forth, though understood from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), are connected with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

This is because its occurrence as delimited by the property of being Caitra (caitratva) is understood through the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), thereby ensuring its meaningfulness. Nor is the cognition generated by the verbal suffix—having a general property as its qualifier—superfluous; for that [cognition] is the motivator for the initial application of the nominative case (*prathamā*). Otherwise, the use of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth would result. For it is not merely the denotation of the action (*kṛti*) that is the motivator for that [application]; even in the case of the impersonal (*bhāva*) verbal suffix, as in "Caitra sleeps" (*caitreṇa supyate*), the nominative is justified because the action (*kṛti*) is denoted through the paraphrase (*vivaraṇa*) with the root *kṛ*.

Therefore, the very expression of [the meanings of] agency and so forth is what necessitates the use of the nominative case; whether this occurs through primary denotation (*śakti*) or secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is another matter. Consequently, the meaning of the nominative case is the status of being a factor of action (*kāraka*) that has been expressed [by a suffix]. Nor does the undesired consequence of the nominative arise in cases such as *prasāda āste* ("he sits on the palace") or *pakvaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats the cooked food"), because the locative status and the objective status are already expressed by the *kṛt*-suffixes [in *prasāda* and *pakvam*]. This is because the meaning of the nominative is restricted precisely to agency and objectivity expressed by *tiṅ*-suffixes or particles; thus, even though the locative status is expressed by the *ghañ*-suffix following the root *sad-* in the word *prasāda*, [the nominative is not applied].

Because there is no contradiction with the seventh [case]; for even when the objecthood (*karmatva*) is expressed by the *ktapratyaya* suffix in the word *pakvam*, there is no contradiction with the second case (*dvitīyā*). Examples of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and particles (*nipāta*) have already been demonstrated previously.
Here, a doubt arises regarding the claim that the meaning of the nominative (*prathamā*) is the agency (*kartṛtva*) expressed by verbal suffixes and particles.

But if this is so, then by implication it follows that the nominative case (*prathamā*) occurs when the *kāraka* is expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) or a particle (*nipāta*), whereas the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*) and other cases occur when it is not so expressed. Consequently, while the nominative would be appropriate for Caitra and others when they are construed with the meaning of the verbal suffix, if one intends to express their connection with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) conveyed by a *kṛt* suffix whose meaning is the agent (*kartṛ*), then the instrumental case would necessarily follow. Thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage: "caitreṇa pācako bhuṅkte" ("Caitra, the cook, eats"). For it is not the case that...

There is no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) of the *kārakas* with the *bhāvanā* expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix. This is because in examples such as "the cooker of rice with wood in a pot eats the food," we observe the connection of the wood and other factors. Therefore, since the connection of the agent-*kāraka* is likewise established there, and since the nominative case is unaccountable due to the absence of an intention to connect it with the action expressed by the finite verb (*tiṅ*), the instrumental case—denoting agency not already expressed by a finite verb—is unavoidable for Caitra, who is intended to be connected with the action expressed by the *kṛt*-suffix.

In this way, there would also be the undesirable consequence of using the accusative case in the sentence, "odanaṃ pakvo bhujyate caitreṇa" (The cooked rice is eaten by Caitra), because the status of being an object (*karmatva*) as defined by the act of cooking (*pāka*) is not expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Furthermore, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in that case would be: "The agent of eating is the locus of the effort conducive to the cooking performed by Caitra. And a double cognition of agency—like [the cognition] "A pot possesses potness"—is not untenable. If it is argued that, likewise, in the case of "odanaṃ pakvo bhujyate," the verbal cognition and the double cognition of objecthood (*karmatva*) should be understood accordingly, then the following is the resolution of the aforementioned doubt: [The resolution: It is not so. For the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) expresses the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) of the act of eating (*bhujana*) with respect to the act of cooking (*pāka*), and it does not express the agenthood of the act of cooking itself. Therefore, the verbal cognition is: "The agent of the act of eating is the locus of the effort conducive to the cooking performed by Caitra. Thus, there is no double cognition of agency. Similarly, in the case of "odanaṃ pakvo bhujyate," the verbal suffix expresses the objecthood of the act of eating with respect to the act of cooking, and not the objecthood of the act of cooking itself. Therefore, the verbal cognition is: "The object of the act of eating is the locus of the effort conducive to the cooking of the rice. Thus, there is no double cognition of objecthood. Consequently, the aforementioned objection is refuted.

The term *anabhihite* (when not already expressed) means "when [the agent or object] has not been expressed by the *kṛt*-suffixes and so forth that are connected with its own [referent]. Consequently, since the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) and the object (*karmatva*) have already been expressed there by the *kṛt*-suffix, there is no possibility of the occurrence of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and so on. As for the first case (*prathamā*), however, there is simply an absence of a cause when one intends to express its connection [with those meanings]. Nor does this imply that the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would occur when one intends to express that connection.

It should not be argued that because the governing rule *anabhihite* is interrupted by the sūtra prescribing the nominative case, it does not carry over into the sūtra *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* which prescribes the genitive for the agent; for it is universally accepted that it does indeed carry over there as well, according to the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*).

Otherwise, when one ought to say "Caitra, the cook, eats" (*caitraḥ pācako bhuṅkte*), there would result the unintended usage "Caitra’s cook eats" (*caitrasya pācako bhuṅkte*). Therefore, in the expression "Caitra, the cook," both nominative forms are construed with the verb "eats" alone; the cognition of mutual identity (*abheda-anvaya*) between them occurs as before. Even where a verbal root is not heard, the verb "is" (*asti*) must be supplied according to the rule *astir bhavantīparaḥ*. As for the objection that there would be an absence of a finite suffix (*tiṅ*) in the present tense (*laṭ*), that is refuted as follows: [the suffix is present in the sense of the verb being understood].

Furthermore, since the nominative case (*prathamā*) is not caused by coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with either a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) or a particle (*nipāta*), then in the stage where "caitraḥ pac" remains (without a suffix), the nominative would be absent. Consequently, because the condition for the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes—namely, being a word that is not coreferential with the nominative (*aprathamā-samānādhikaraṇa-pada*)—would be present, the specific rule "the *śatṛ* and *śānac* replace the *laṭ* when not coreferential with the nominative" (*laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāvaprathamā-samānādhikaraṇe*) would result in the application of those very suffixes (*śatṛ* and *śānac*) instead of the *laṭ*.

It cannot be argued that because the *tiṅ* suffixes and so forth have as their sole domain the *liṭ* and other such [perfect] endings, their application in the present tense (*laṭ*) would be untenable due to the force of a general rule; for such an interpretation is established by the prescription of the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes in the *laṭ*. Otherwise, the phrase "not coreferential with the nominative" (*aprathamā-samānādhikaraṇa*) would become redundant. To avoid this redundancy, it is established by the force of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the nominative case exists even in the *laṭ*; and since that [nominative] is untenable without coreferentiality with the *tiṅ* suffixes and so forth which serve as the indicators [of person and number], the existence of *tiṅ* suffixes in the *laṭ* is logically established.

For this very reason, it is indicated by the *jñāpaka* that all case-endings (*vibhakti*) occur in the present tense (*laṭ*), taking the future tense markers such as *tiṅ* and others as their cause. And although the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are prescribed there in coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a nominative (*prathamā*) non-different case-ending, they do not have the power to sublate the previously established *tiṅ* endings and so forth. Thus, even if the phrase "not in coreferentiality with a non-nominative" (*aprathamā-samānādhikaraṇe*) is interpreted as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the occurrence of *tiṅ* endings and the like in the present tense is justified; this is even more so under the view that it is a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

The arguments regarding the resolution of the derivation of *tiṅ* suffixes and so forth in the *laṭ* [present tense] as presented by the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* have not been written here, as they are difficult to manage. In any case, he states that the nominative occurs when both agenthood and objecthood are expressed by either a *tiṅ* suffix or a particle (*nipāta*). Furthermore, it is established that the connection of these two with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) conveyed by the verb is exactly like the connection of the meanings of the accusative and other cases with the meaning of the verbal root. Nor should it be argued: "Even if this is so, the meaning of the nominative connects only with the meaning of the verb, whereas the meaning of the accusative and others connects even with the meaning of the *kṛt* suffixes and so forth; how then can there be identity between cause and effect?"

Even though the cognition produced by a word that is not syntactically connected with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is a cause—by way of the relation of being the qualificandum of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—for that which is delimited by the state of being verbal knowledge whose qualifier is the object denoted by the suffix, the attainment of the specific [qualifier] is nonetheless possible through other causes, such as the cognition of what has been expressed by another means of knowledge or the like; this is the general direction [of the argument].
Thus ends the determination of the meaning of the nominative case according to the view of Kātyāyana, in the *Bhaṭṭatantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Khaṇḍadeva.
